text:
A data organization leader is upset about the data analysis team’s reports being different from the data
engineering team’s reports. The leader believes the siloed nature of their organization’s data engineering and
data analysis architectures is to blame.Which of the following describes how a data lakehouse could alleviate
this issue?

choices.text:
Both teams would autoscale their work as data
size evolves

Both teams would use the same source of truth for
their work

Both teams would reorganize to report to the
same department

Both teams would be able to collaborate on
projects in real-time

Both teams would respond more quickly to ad-
hoc requests

originalKeyText:
b) Both teams would use the
same source of truth for
their work

explanations.a:
Autoscaling changes compute capacity; it does not make the two teams read the same data.

Additional context:
Autoscaling is appropriate when workload demand grows or shrinks. Report consistency still depends on reading the same governed source.
explanations.b:
A shared source of truth directly addresses reports diverging because engineering and analytics maintain separate architectures.

Additional context:
The scenario’s clue is disagreement caused by architecture silos. Reusing shared governed data removes that separate-copy cause rather than only making each report faster.
explanations.c:
A lakehouse is a data architecture; reorganizing reporting lines is not its mechanism for consistency.

Additional context:
Reporting-line changes are an organizational intervention. They do not establish a shared table version or consistent source values.
explanations.d:
Real-time collaboration can help teams work together, but does not itself reconcile separate copies of reporting data.

Additional context:
Collaborative editing is useful when coauthoring notebooks or queries. It is not equivalent to replacing inconsistent reporting datasets with one source of truth.
explanations.e:
Faster ad hoc responses concern responsiveness; the problem here is consistency between separate reporting sources.

Additional context:
Ad hoc responsiveness is useful for analysis turnaround. A fast report can still disagree with another report that reads a different copy.

references.title: What is a data lakehouse?
references.section: What is a data lakehouse used for?
references.support: A lakehouse lets engineering and analytics use a shared source of truth instead of maintaining inconsistent silos.

keyConcept: A lakehouse lets engineering and analytics use a shared source of truth instead of maintaining inconsistent silos.
examTip: When reports disagree because teams use separate data stores, look for shared data rather than faster compute.
analysis: A lakehouse lets engineering and analytics use a shared source of truth instead of maintaining inconsistent silos.

text: Which of the following describes a scenario in which a data team will want to utilize cluster pools?

choices.text:
An automated report needs to be refreshed as
quickly as possible

An automated report needs to be made
reproducible

An automated report needs to be tested to
identify errors

An automated report needs to be version-
controlled across multiple collaborators

An automated report needs to be runnable by all
stakeholders

originalKeyText:
a) An automated report needs
to be refreshed as quickly
as possible

explanations.a: A report that must refresh quickly benefits when its job cluster can obtain already available pool instances. A pool targets provisioning time rather than changing the query result.
explanations.b: Reproducibility depends on controlled code, runtime, and inputs. Keeping instances idle does not version or freeze those dependencies.
explanations.c: Tests and data quality rules detect incorrect behavior. A pool supplies compute instances and does not run correctness assertions on the report.
explanations.d: Git folders manage branches and commits across collaborators. Instance reuse does not provide version control.
explanations.e: Who can run a report is controlled by permissions. Pool membership does not grant every stakeholder access to the report or underlying data.

text: Which of the following is hosted completely in the control plane of the classic Databricks architecture?

choices.text: Worker node
JDBC data source
Databricks web application
Databricks Filesystem
Driver node

originalKeyText: c) Databricks web application

explanations.a:
A worker executes distributed processing in the classic compute plane, rather than being hosted entirely in the control plane.

Additional context:
Workers execute tasks and process workload data. Classic workers reside in the customer compute plane rather than the central web-application service.
explanations.b:
A JDBC data source is an external system being queried; using a connector does not make the source a control-plane application.

Additional context:
JDBC is a connectivity interface to a data system. An external database does not move into the control plane merely because Databricks queries it.
explanations.c:
The architecture documentation explicitly locates the Databricks web application in the control plane.

Additional context:
The architecture reference explicitly identifies the web application as control-plane hosted. This distinguishes user-facing management from Spark execution.
explanations.d:
The filesystem represents data storage access, rather than the control-plane web application; classic workspace storage is associated with the customer cloud account.

Additional context:
Storage access and the workspace storage bucket are distinct from hosting the web UI. Do not classify a filesystem namespace as the control-plane application.
explanations.e:
The driver is part of classic compute execution in the compute plane, not the control-plane web application.

Additional context:
The driver coordinates a Spark application on compute. It is not the management web application hosted by the control plane.

references.title: High-level architecture
references.section: Workspace architecture
references.support: The Databricks web application is in the Databricks-managed control plane; classic compute nodes run in the customer compute plane.

keyConcept: The Databricks web application is in the Databricks-managed control plane; classic compute nodes run in the customer compute plane.
examTip: For classic architecture, distinguish the workspace UI from the driver and workers that execute workloads.
analysis: The Databricks web application is in the Databricks-managed control plane; classic compute nodes run in the customer compute plane.

text: Which of the following benefits of using the Databricks Lakehouse Platform is provided by Delta Lake?

choices.text:
The ability to manipulate the same data using a
variety of languages

The ability to collaborate in real time on a single
notebook
The ability to set up alerts for query failures

The ability to support batch and streaming
workloads
The ability to distribute complex data operations

originalKeyText:
d) The ability to support batch
and streaming workloads

explanations.a:
Multiple programming languages are a notebook/Spark interface capability; they are not the distinctive storage guarantee supplied by Delta Lake.

Additional context:
Notebook language selection and Spark APIs let developers choose Python, SQL, Scala, or R where supported. That interface choice is not the Delta storage layer’s distinctive benefit here.
explanations.b:
Collaborative notebook editing is a workspace feature, rather than a Delta Lake storage feature.

Additional context:
Coauthoring improves team development workflows. It is separate from the guarantees of transaction-log-backed table storage.
explanations.c:
Query failure alerts belong to monitoring and orchestration, not the Delta Lake storage layer.

Additional context:
Alerts monitor query outcomes or result conditions. They belong to workflow/SQL services rather than being supplied by a Delta data file.
explanations.d:
The Delta Lake overview explicitly describes tight Structured Streaming integration and using a single copy for batch and streaming operations.

Additional context:
The scenario asks which platform benefit is attributable specifically to Delta Lake. Its single-table batch/streaming integration is expressly documented.
explanations.e:
Distributing execution across compute resources is Spark’s role; Delta Lake adds transactional storage and metadata.

Additional context:
Spark distributes execution across tasks and workers. Delta complements that engine with transactional tables, not with the engine’s general distribution mechanism.

text: Which of the following describes the storage organization of a Delta table?

choices.text:
Delta tables are stored in a single file that contains
data, history, metadata, and other attributes

Delta tables store their data in a single file and all
metadata in a collection of files in a separate
location

Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that
contain data, history, metadata, and other
attributes

Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that
contain only the data stored within the table

Delta tables are stored in a single file that contains
only the data stored within the table

originalKeyText:
c) Delta tables are stored in a
collection of files that
contain data, history,
metadata, and other
attributes

explanations.a:
A Delta table is not a single file containing everything; it consists of data files plus a transaction log.

Additional context:
A table directory may contain many Parquet files and log/checkpoint metadata. One file is not the unit that stores the entire table history.
explanations.b:
Although metadata is separate from data files, the table’s data is not restricted to one data file.

Additional context:
A growing table can have multiple active data files. Separating metadata from data does not imply that only one data file holds all rows.
explanations.c:
A collection of files containing data and transaction metadata matches Delta’s Parquet files plus transaction log.

Additional context:
The transaction log records table state and actions while Parquet files hold rows. Together they form the file collection described by this option.
explanations.d:
Data-only files omit the transaction log and metadata needed for table versions and ACID behavior.

Additional context:
Without transaction metadata, a directory of data files is not sufficient to supply Delta versions and ACID semantics. Data-only layout omits the feature being tested.
explanations.e:
A single data-only file omits both the multi-file data layout and the transaction metadata.

Additional context:
A single file can be part of a tiny snapshot but is not the Delta table storage model. The question asks about the model, not an accidental small-table file count.

references.title: What is Delta Lake in Databricks?
references.section: What is Delta Lake in Databricks?
references.support: Delta tables use Parquet data files plus a file-based transaction log, rather than one all-in-one file.

keyConcept: Delta tables use Parquet data files plus a file-based transaction log, rather than one all-in-one file.
examTip: Distinguish a table directory with data and transaction metadata from an individual data file.
analysis: Delta tables use Parquet data files plus a file-based transaction log, rather than one all-in-one file.

text:
Which of the following code blocks will remove the rows where the value in column age is greater than 25
from the existing Delta table my table and save the updated table?

choices.text: SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE age > 25;
UPDATE my_table WHERE age > 25;
DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age > 25;
UPDATE my_table WHERE age <= 25;
DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age <= 25;

originalKeyText:
c) DELETE FROM my_table
WHERE age > 25;

explanations.a:
SELECT reads the rows where age > 25; it does not remove or persist changes to those rows.

Additional context:
SELECT is suitable for inspecting which records match before deletion. It does not commit a DELETE to the target table.
explanations.b:
UPDATE is for changing column values, and this statement supplies no SET assignment or delete operation.

Additional context:
Use UPDATE ... SET when values in existing records need changing. Removing records instead calls for DELETE FROM with the requested predicate.
explanations.c:
DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age > 25 removes exactly the requested rows and commits the table change.

Additional context:
The condition is strictly greater than 25, so age 25 is retained. The committed delete removes matching rows from the current logical table state.
explanations.d:
UPDATE neither deletes rows nor supplies a SET clause; its age <= 25 predicate also targets the opposite group.

Additional context:
Even a syntactically complete UPDATE would change values rather than delete records. This predicate also selects the wrong side of the age boundary.
explanations.e:
This DELETE targets ages 25 and below, which is the complement of the requested age > 25 condition.

Additional context:
This would remove the records that should remain. Checking the predicate direction is as important as selecting the correct DML verb.

references.title: DELETE FROM
references.section: Syntax; Parameters — WHERE
references.support: DELETE FROM removes rows matching its WHERE predicate from a Delta table.

keyConcept: DELETE FROM removes rows matching its WHERE predicate from a Delta table.
examTip: Translate “remove rows greater than 25” into DELETE with age > 25.
analysis: DELETE FROM removes rows matching its WHERE predicate from a Delta table.

text:
A data engineer has realized that they made a mistake when making a daily update to a table. They need to
use Delta time travel to restore the table to a version that is 3 days old. However, when the data engineer
attempts to time travel to the older version, they are unable to restore the data because the data files have
been deleted.
Which of the following explains why the data files are no longer present?

choices.text: The VACUUM command was run on the table
The TIME TRAVEL command was run on the table

The DELETE HISTORY command was run on the
table
The OPTIMIZE command was nun on the table
The HISTORY command was run on the table

originalKeyText:
a) The VACUUM command was
run on the table
issues: Ambiguous retention assumption: VACUUM can remove history files, but its default retention is 7 days, not 3. The question does not specify a shortened retention policy.

explanations.a: VACUUM is the listed operation that physically removes eligible obsolete files. However, a normal seven-day retention would not explain deletion of files needed for this three-day-old version; additional configuration is required.
explanations.b: Time travel reads an earlier snapshot and does not delete its files. It needs both the transaction history and referenced data files to remain available.
explanations.c: DELETE HISTORY is not the documented Delta maintenance command for removing old physical data files. Do not substitute an invented command for VACUUM.
explanations.d: OPTIMIZE rewrites active files for layout and compaction while retaining old files for concurrent readers and history. Physical cleanup is subsequently governed by retention and VACUUM.
explanations.e: DESCRIBE HISTORY reports commits rather than removing data. Inspecting history cannot by itself explain missing physical files.

references.title: Remove unused data files with vacuum
references.section: Caveats for vacuum; Configure data retention
references.support: VACUUM can physically remove obsolete data files and prevent time travel, but the default file retention is seven days. A three-day-old restore failure needs an unstated shorter retention or other deletion, so the provided scenario is underspecified.

references.title: Work with table history
references.section: Caveats for vacuum; Configure data retention
references.support: VACUUM can physically remove obsolete data files and prevent time travel, but the default file retention is seven days. A three-day-old restore failure needs an unstated shorter retention or other deletion, so the provided scenario is underspecified.

analysis: VACUUM can physically remove obsolete data files and prevent time travel, but the default file retention is seven days. A three-day-old restore failure needs an unstated shorter retention or other deletion, so the provided scenario is underspecified.
keyConcept: VACUUM can physically remove obsolete data files and prevent time travel, but the default file retention is seven days. A three-day-old restore failure needs an unstated shorter retention or other deletion, so the provided scenario is underspecified.
examTip: Check both log retention and data-file retention; never infer a three-day retention policy from default VACUUM behavior.

text: Which of the following data lakehouse features results in improved data quality over a traditional data lake?

choices.text:
A data lakehouse provides storage solutions for
structured and unstructured data

A data lakehouse supports ACID-compliant
transactions

A data lakehouse allows the use of SQL queries to
examine data
A data lakehouse stores data in open formats

A data lakehouse enables machine learning and
artificial Intelligence workloads

originalKeyText:
b) A data lakehouse supports
ACID-compliant
transactions

explanations.a: Handling structured and unstructured data describes broad storage support. Traditional lakes can already hold both, so this does not isolate the quality improvement.
explanations.b: ACID-compliant transactions keep writes atomic and reads consistent as data changes. The lakehouse documentation identifies Delta transactional storage and schema enforcement as core improvements.
explanations.c: SQL makes data accessible to analysts but does not itself make incomplete or conflicting writes transactional. A query interface is distinct from a quality guarantee.
explanations.d: Open formats improve interoperability and reduce dependence on one engine. Openness alone does not validate data or enforce atomic updates.
explanations.e: ML and AI workloads describe consumers of stored data. Supporting those workloads does not by itself prevent unreliable records or inconsistent table updates.

Databricks Repos is wholly housed within the

text:
A data engineer has left the organization. The data team needs to transfer ownership of the data engineer's
Delta tables to a new data engineer. The new data engineer is the lead engineer on the data team. Assuming
the original data engineer no longer has access, which of the following individuals must be the one to transfer
ownership of the Delta tables in Data Explorer?

choices.text: Databricks account representative
This transfer is not possible
Workspace administrator
New lead data engineer
Original data engineer

originalKeyText: c) Workspace administrator

explanations.a: A commercial account representative is not automatically a data-object administrator. An organizational contact role does not confer table ownership privileges.
explanations.b: Ownership transfer is supported by ALTER ... OWNER TO and Catalog Explorer. The owner leaving does not make transfer impossible.
explanations.c: Workspace admin is the expected answer in a legacy table-ACL context. It is not a universal exclusive authority for Unity Catalog tables, which is why the question remains conditional.
explanations.d: Being the lead engineer does not automatically grant transfer privileges. The new engineer needs an applicable administrative, ownership, or MANAGE authority.
explanations.e: An existing owner can normally transfer ownership, but this person no longer has access. Recovery must use another authorized principal rather than require the departed owner.

text:
A data analyst has created a Delta table sales that is used by the entire data analysis team. They want help
from the data engineering team to implement a series of tests to ensure the data is clean. However, the data
engineering team uses Python for its tests rather than SQL. Which of the following commands could the data
engineering team use to access sales in PySpark?

choices.text: SELECT * FROM sales

There is no way to share data between PySpark
and SQL
spark.sql("sales")
spark.delta.table("sales")
spark.table("sales")

originalKeyText: e) spark.table("sales")

explanations.a: SELECT is valid SQL syntax but this bare text is not the requested Python command. Wrap a full SELECT query in spark.sql when using it in a Python cell.
explanations.b: Databricks exposes tables through SQL and DataFrame APIs. There is no separate SQL-only physical copy that prevents Python access.
explanations.c: spark.sql expects a SQL statement rather than just the identifier sales. spark.sql("SELECT * FROM sales") would be a valid alternative, but it is not the printed option.
explanations.d: spark.delta.table is not the documented SparkSession table reader. Delta storage is read through standard table/DataFrame APIs.
explanations.e: spark.table("sales") loads the registered table as a DataFrame. Python assertions can then inspect the same records used by the SQL team.

text: Which of the following commands will return the location of database customer360?

choices.text: DESCRIBE LOCATION customer360;
DROP DATABASE customer360;
DESCRIBE DATABASE customer360;

ALTER DATABASE customer360 SET
DBPROPERTIES ('location' = '/user'};
USE DATABASE customer360;

originalKeyText:
c) DESCRIBE DATABASE
customer360;

explanations.a: DESCRIBE LOCATION is not the documented schema-inspection syntax. The object type is DATABASE or SCHEMA, followed by its name.
explanations.b: DROP DATABASE removes the schema rather than reporting its location. It is a destructive operation and does not answer the inspection request.
explanations.c: DESCRIBE DATABASE customer360 returns the schema name, comment, and location. The official reference explicitly treats DATABASE and SCHEMA as synonyms.
explanations.d: ALTER changes metadata rather than reporting it, and a DBPROPERTIES string is not a location-inspection command. This option also has malformed punctuation.
explanations.e: USE DATABASE changes name resolution for subsequent statements. It does not display the schema’s storage metadata.

references.title: DESCRIBE SCHEMA
references.section: Syntax; Examples
references.support: DESCRIBE SCHEMA returns metadata including the filesystem location; DATABASE is an interchangeable synonym. It inspects rather than changes the schema.

analysis: DESCRIBE SCHEMA returns metadata including the filesystem location; DATABASE is an interchangeable synonym. It inspects rather than changes the schema.
keyConcept: DESCRIBE SCHEMA returns metadata including the filesystem location; DATABASE is an interchangeable synonym. It inspects rather than changes the schema.
examTip: A request to report a location calls for DESCRIBE, not USE, ALTER, or DROP.

text:
A data engineer wants to create a new table containing the names of customers that live in France. They
have written the following command:
CREATE TABLE customersInFrance
AS
SELECT id, firstName, lastName
FROM customerLocations
WHERE country = 'FRANCE';
A senior data engineer mentions that it is organization policy to include a table property indicating that the
new table includes personally identifiable information (PII). Which of the following lines of code fills in the
above blank to successfully complete the task?

choices.text:
There is no way to indicate whether a table
contains PII
"COMMENT PII"
TBLPROPERTIES PII
COMMENT "Contains PII"
PII

originalKeyText: d) COMMENT "Contains PII"

explanations.a: A table can carry a COMMENT and other supported metadata. The platform does not prevent documenting that a table contains PII.
explanations.b: Quoting COMMENT PII makes it a string literal rather than a COMMENT clause. SQL needs the clause keyword outside the quoted description.
explanations.c: TBLPROPERTIES requires parenthesized key/value pairs, not a bare PII token. A valid property could be used in another statement, but this fragment is malformed.
explanations.d: COMMENT "Contains PII" is the supported metadata clause among the choices. The source’s missing blank must be placed in the CREATE TABLE clauses before AS SELECT; the comment alone does not enforce privacy.
explanations.e: PII by itself is not a CREATE TABLE clause. Meaningful human labels still need valid SQL metadata syntax.

references.title: CREATE TABLE [USING]
references.section: Parameters — COMMENT; AS query
references.support: CREATE TABLE accepts a COMMENT string that documents the table. It is metadata for discoverability, not a security control or automatic PII classifier.

analysis: CREATE TABLE accepts a COMMENT string that documents the table. It is metadata for discoverability, not a security control or automatic PII classifier.
keyConcept: CREATE TABLE accepts a COMMENT string that documents the table. It is metadata for discoverability, not a security control or automatic PII classifier.
examTip: Distinguish documentation metadata from governance controls that actually restrict PII access.

text: Which of the following benefits is provided by the array functions from Spark SQL?

choices.text:
An ability to work with data in a variety of types at
once

text:
Which of the following commands can be used to write data into a Delta table while avoiding the writing of
duplicate records?

choices.text: DROP
IGNORE
MERGE
APPEND
INSERT

originalKeyText: c) MERGE

explanations.a: DROP removes a table or object rather than merging records safely. It cannot append new unique data while preserving the target.
explanations.b: IGNORE is not the standalone Delta write operation that matches incoming business keys. Ignoring an existing object or error is not record-level deduplication.
explanations.c: MERGE can use WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT so previously present keys are not inserted again. The documentation separately warns that duplicates inside the incoming batch need deduplication.
explanations.d: APPEND adds incoming rows without automatically comparing them to existing keys. Replaying a batch can therefore create duplicate records.

text:
A data analyst has a series of queries in a SQL program. The data analyst wants this program to run every
day. They only want the final query in the program to run on Sundays. They ask for help from the data
engineering team to complete this task.
Which of the following approaches could be used by the data engineering team to complete this task?

choices.text:
They could submit a feature request with
Databricks to add this functionality

They could wrap the queries using PySpark and
use Python’s control flow system to determine
when to run the final query

They could only run the entire program on
Sundays

They could automatically restrict access to the
source table in the final query so that it is only
accessible on Sundays

They could redesign the data model to separate
the data used in the final query into a new table

originalKeyText:
b) They could wrap the
queries using PySpark and
use Python’s control flow
system to determine when
to run the final query

explanations.a: The platform already supports Python orchestration of SQL, so a feature request is unnecessary. Notebook language support is not restricted to one rigid SQL program.
explanations.b: Wrapping SQL execution in Python allows a weekday check to guard the final query. Earlier statements can still run on every daily execution.
explanations.c: Running the entire program only on Sundays would skip required daily queries. It changes the schedule of every statement instead of only the last one.
explanations.d: Changing access permissions is a security operation rather than ordinary program control flow. It would also affect other consumers of the table.
explanations.e: Separating tables changes the data model but does not by itself decide when a query runs. The requirement concerns execution logic, not storage layout.

text:
A data engineer runs a statement every day to copy the previous day’s sales into the table transactions.
Each day’s sales are in their own file in the location "/transactions/raw".
Today, the data engineer runs the following command to complete this task:
COPY INTO TRANSACTIONS
FROM "/transactions/raw"
FILEFORMAT = PARQUET;
After running the command today, the data engineer notices that the number of records in table
transactions has not changed.
Which of the following describes why the statement might not have copied any new records into the table?

choices.text:
The format of the files to be copied were not
included with the FORMAT_OPTIONS keyword

The names of the files to be copied were not
included with the FILES keyword

The previous day’s file has already been copied
into the table

The PARQUET file format does not support COPY
INTO

The COPY INTO statement requires the table to
be refreshed to view the copied rows

originalKeyText:
c) The previous day’s file has
already been copied into
the table

explanations.a: FILEFORMAT specifies Parquet; FORMAT_OPTIONS is for optional format settings. The absence of FORMAT_OPTIONS does not prevent all Parquet ingestion.
explanations.b: COPY INTO can discover source files from a location without an explicit FILES list. File selection options are not a mandatory list of every filename.
explanations.c: An already loaded file is skipped by the normal idempotent behavior. That explains an unchanged target count on a repeated run without assuming a syntax failure.
explanations.d: Parquet is explicitly a supported COPY INTO source format. Its use is not a reason the command cannot ingest records.
explanations.e: A refresh command is not the mechanism that makes a committed COPY visible in the Delta table. Skipped input files explain why no new rows were written.

examTip: When a repeated COPY INTO adds no rows, check file ingestion history before assuming a refresh or file-format error.

text:
A data engineering team has two tables. The first table march_transactions is a collection of all retail
transactions in the month of March. The second table april_transactions is a collection of all retail
transactions in the month of April. There are no duplicate records between the tables.
Which of the following commands should be run to create a new table all_transactions that contains all
records from march_transactions and april_transactions without duplicate records?
originalKeyText:
b) CREATE TABLE
all_transactions AS
SELECT FROM
march_transactions
UNION SELECT FROM
april_transactions;

explanations.a: INNER JOIN combines matching row pairs and requires a valid query and join structure. It is not a vertical concatenation of March and April transactions.
explanations.b: UNION is conceptually appropriate and removes duplicate rows by default. As printed, SELECT FROM supplies no projection; a supported repair would be SELECT * FROM each table, but that repair is not in the original choice.
explanations.c: An outer join combines rows across related columns, not a simple union of the two months. This option is also syntactically incomplete.
explanations.d: INTERSECT returns rows common to both inputs. The question says there are no duplicates between months, so intersection does not produce all transactions.
explanations.e: MERGE is a data-modification statement, not a set operator placed between these SELECT fragments. It does not supply the requested CTAS union syntax.

text:
A data engineer only wants to execute the final block of a Python program if the Python variable
day_of_week is equal to 1 and the Python variable review_period is True.
Which of the following control flow statements should the data engineer use to begin this conditionally
executed code block?

if day_of_week = 1 and review_period = "True":
if day_of_week == 1 and review_period == "True":
if day_of_week == 1 and review_period:
if day_of_week = 1 & review_period: = "True":

originalKeyText:

review_period:

explanations.a: A uses assignment syntax where the if condition requires a comparison. It cannot test whether day_of_week equals 1 as written.
explanations.b: B contains assignments inside the condition and compares to a quoted string rather than the Boolean value. Both syntax and intended value checks are wrong.
explanations.c: C has the correct day comparison but tests review_period against the string "True". A Boolean True is not that string, so this would not implement the requirement.
explanations.d: D combines day_of_week == 1 with the truth value of review_period. Both conditions must hold before the indented block runs.
explanations.e: E combines invalid assignment punctuation with a bitwise operator. It is not the Boolean conjunction and equality test the scenario requires.

text:
A data engineer is attempting to drop a Spark SQL table my_table. The data engineer wants to delete all
table metadata and data.
They run the following command:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS my_table -
While the object no longer appears when they run SHOW TABLES, the data files still exist.
Which of the following describes why the data files still exist and the metadata files were deleted?

choices.text: The table’s data was larger than 10 GB
The table’s data was smaller than 10 GB
The table was external
The table did not have a location
The table was managed

originalKeyText: c) The table was external

explanations.a: There is no 10-GB cutoff in the documented DROP TABLE external-table rule. Size does not convert a managed table to external.
explanations.b: Small table size likewise does not explain metadata-only deletion. The managed-versus-external distinction is the relevant condition.
explanations.c: External table data is left in place when the table definition is dropped. This directly matches disappearing catalog metadata with retained source files.
explanations.d: A table still has a data location; not explicitly writing LOCATION in SQL is not a general explanation for retained files. Storage ownership is determined by the table type.
explanations.e: Managed table data is subject to platform lifecycle management when dropped, including delayed recovery/purge behavior in Unity Catalog. Metadata-only retention of external files is the external-table rule.

Function
View
Temporary view
Table

originalKeyText: e) Table

explanations.a: A database or schema groups objects and is not itself the result relation created from two tables. It does not materialize that join or query result.
explanations.b: A function defines reusable computation. It is not the persistent stored relation the question requests.
explanations.c: An ordinary view can be shared across sessions but does not store a physical copy of its query result. That misses the materialization requirement.
explanations.d: A temporary view is scoped to its creating session. It fails the explicit requirement that other engineers use the object from other sessions.
explanations.e: A persistent table created from the query stores the result and can be queried in other sessions. This satisfies both durability and physical data requirements.

text:
A data engineer is maintaining a data pipeline. Upon data ingestion, the data engineer notices that the

Data Explorer
Delta Lake
Delta Live Tables
Auto Loader

originalKeyText: d) Delta Live Tables

explanations.a: Unity Catalog controls governance and access to data objects. Governance alone does not define the source record quality rules described here.
explanations.b: Data Explorer browses objects and metadata. It is not the pipeline execution feature that evaluates each row against a declared expectation.
explanations.c: Delta Lake provides transactional table storage and schema enforcement. The named managed-pipeline feature for richer expectation metrics is DLT/Lakeflow.
explanations.d: DLT/Lakeflow expectations evaluate Boolean quality constraints and report retained or dropped invalid rows. They are directly intended for automated pipeline data quality monitoring.
explanations.e: Auto Loader ingests newly arriving files and manages schema evolution. It is not the expectation framework for arbitrary business-quality checks across transformed tables.

text:
In order for Structured Streaming to reliably track the exact progress of the processing so that it can handle
any kind of failure by restarting and/or reprocessing, which of the following two approaches is used by Spark
to record the offset range of the data being processed in each trigger?

choices.text: Checkpointing and Write-ahead Logs

Structured Streaming cannot record the offset
range of the data being processed in each trigger.
Replayable Sources and Idempotent Sinks
Write-ahead Logs and Idempotent Sinks
Checkpointing and Idempotent Sinks

originalKeyText:
a) Checkpointing and Write-
ahead Logs

explanations.a: Checkpoint state includes per-batch source offsets and commits, working with write-ahead logs for recovery. That is the documented progress bookkeeping requested.
explanations.b: The checkpoint documentation explicitly describes recorded source offsets. Structured Streaming can therefore resume from recorded progress.
explanations.c: Replayable sources and idempotent sinks help achieve reliable end-to-end processing. They are not the two state-recording structures named in this question.
explanations.d: An idempotent sink prevents repeated output effects, while a write-ahead log records progress. This pairing omits the checkpoint information explicitly requested.
explanations.e: Checkpointing records progress, but sink idempotency is an output behavior rather than an offset log. The question asks for the two bookkeeping mechanisms together.

references.section: Structured Streaming checkpoints
references.support: Structured Streaming uses checkpoints and write-ahead logs to record offsets, committed batches, and recovery state. Replayable sources and idempotent sinks are complementary guarantees rather than the two progress-recording mechanisms asked for.

analysis: Structured Streaming uses checkpoints and write-ahead logs to record offsets, committed batches, and recovery state. Replayable sources and idempotent sinks are complementary guarantees rather than the two progress-recording mechanisms asked for.
keyConcept: Structured Streaming uses checkpoints and write-ahead logs to record offsets, committed batches, and recovery state. Replayable sources and idempotent sinks are complementary guarantees rather than the two progress-recording mechanisms asked for.
examTip: If the question asks what records offset progress, look for checkpoint and log state, not only sink behavior.

text: Which of the following describes the relationship between Gold tables and Silver tables?

choices.text:
Gold tables are more likely to contain
aggregations than Silver tables.

Gold tables are more likely to contain valuable
data than Silver tables.

Gold tables are more likely to contain a less
refined view of data than Silver tables.

Gold tables are more likely to contain more data
than Silver tables.

Gold tables are more likely to contain truthful
data than Silver tables.

originalKeyText:
a) Gold tables are more likely
to contain aggregations
than Silver tables.

explanations.a:
Gold commonly contains aggregates tailored to reporting, whereas Silver retains validated detailed records.

Additional context:
Gold is tailored to business questions such as weekly sales or customer spending. Silver normally retains validated detailed records that those aggregates use.
explanations.b:
“More valuable” is subjective and is not the documented distinction between these layers.

Additional context:
Both layers can be valuable to different consumers. Value judgments are not a technical definition that determines layer placement.
explanations.c:
Gold is highly refined for downstream use, rather than a less refined form of Silver.

Additional context:
Gold adds a business-serving shape on top of cleaned data. It does not deliberately degrade the data quality of Silver.
explanations.d:
Aggregation often reduces row counts; Gold is not defined by containing more data than Silver.

Additional context:
A summary can have fewer rows than its inputs, while modeling can change shapes in other ways. No universal row-count ordering defines the layers.

Bronze tables contain less data than raw data

Databricks SQL

Streaming

Additional context:
Checkpointing is essential for progress and recovery state. It works with Structured Streaming rather than replacing the processing framework.
explanations.b:
Auto Loader provides a Structured Streaming source called cloudFiles, making Structured Streaming the incremental processing mechanism.

Additional context:
cloudFiles integrates file discovery into the streaming read API. The source can run continuously or in a bounded AvailableNow catch-up.
explanations.c:
Data Explorer is a catalog browsing interface, not an incremental file processing engine.

Additional context:
The explorer is appropriate for inspecting catalog tables and metadata. It is not the runtime source that notices and ingests arriving files.
explanations.d:

Additional context:

explanations.e:
Databricks SQL is a SQL analytics interface; the engine used by Auto Loader’s cloudFiles source is Structured Streaming.

text:
A data engineer has configured a Structured Streaming job to read from a table, manipulate the data, and
then perform a streaming write into a new table.
The code block used by the data engineer is on he left:
If the data engineer only wants the query to process all of the available data in as many batches as required,
which of the following lines of code should the data engineer use to fill in the blank?

choices.text: processingTime(1)
trigger(availableNow=True)
trigger(parallelBatch=True)
trigger(processingTime="once")
trigger(continuous="once")

originalKeyText: b) trigger(availableNow=True)

explanations.a:
processingTime(1) is neither the shown DataStreamWriter trigger syntax nor a bounded catch-up request.

Additional context:
A fixed processing interval would use the named processingTime argument. It does not express terminating after the starting backlog has been processed.
explanations.b:
trigger(availableNow=True) performs bounded incremental processing of available data and supports batch sizing.

Additional context:
The multi-batch wording is the key clue. AvailableNow can respect input-rate limits while eventually finishing the bounded backlog.
explanations.c:
parallelBatch is not a documented trigger option and cannot request AvailableNow processing.

Additional context:
Trigger names must come from the documented API, not plausible English descriptions. No such parallelBatch option is established in the reference.
explanations.d:
processingTime expects a time interval, not the string once, and describes periodic processing rather than a bounded catch-up.

Additional context:
The string once is not a valid processing-time duration. A bounded trigger and a periodic micro-batch interval are different configurations.
explanations.e:
continuous="once" is not the supported bounded trigger. The documentation lists Continuous as unsupported on Databricks.

Additional context:
The documented overview distinguishes AvailableNow from Continuous. A made-up combination of the two names does not create bounded catch-up behavior.

text:
A data engineer has developed a data pipeline to ingest data from a JSON source using Auto Loader, but the
engineer has not provided any type inference or schema hints in their pipeline. Upon reviewing the data, the
data engineer has noticed that all of the columns in the target table are of the string type despite some of
the fields only including float or boolean values.
Which of the following describes why Auto Loader inferred all of the columns to be of the string type?

There was a type mismatch between the specific
schema and the inferred schema
JSON data is a text-based format
Auto Loader only works with string data
All of the fields had at least one null value

Auto Loader cannot infer the schema of ingested
data

originalKeyText:
b) JSON data is a text-based
format
issues: Source options do not accurately explain the default: Auto Loader infers JSON/CSV fields as STRING unless cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes is enabled.

explanations.a: The prompt says no explicit schema was supplied, so a mismatch between a supplied schema and inferred schema is not established. The behavior is explained by the default inference policy.
explanations.b: JSON is textual, but that alone does not prevent typed Boolean or numeric inference. The documented configurable STRING default, omitted here, is the technical reason.
explanations.c: Auto Loader supports typed schemas and can infer column types when configured. Saying it only works with strings is false and makes the supplied C key unreliable.
explanations.d: Nothing in the question establishes a null in every field. Default STRING inference does not depend on all columns containing nulls.
explanations.e: Auto Loader supports schema inference and evolution. The existence of a specific default type policy contradicts the assertion that it cannot infer schemas.

text: Which of the following data workloads will utilize a Gold table as its source?

choices.text:
A job that enriches data by parsing its
timestamps into a human-readable format

A job that aggregates uncleaned data to create
standard summary statistics

A job that cleans data by removing malformatted
records

A job that queries aggregated data designed to
feed into a dashboard

A job that ingests raw data from a streaming
source into the Lakehouse

originalKeyText:
d) A job that queries
aggregated data designed
to feed into a dashboard

explanations.a:
Parsing timestamps is a refinement operation, normally upstream of a report-ready Gold dataset.

Additional context:
Timestamp cleanup/enrichment normally produces a cleaner detailed representation. It is upstream refinement rather than a reason to consume Gold summaries.
explanations.b:
Aggregating uncleaned inputs bypasses the validated Silver stage; it is not a reason to read a Gold source.

Additional context:
Raw invalid data should first pass the appropriate validation stages. Directly summarizing dirty inputs does not make the source a Gold serving dataset.
explanations.c:
Removing malformed records is a cleansing operation associated with Silver, not consumption of Gold aggregates.

Additional context:
Removing malformed records is a quality step. Silver is the documented layer for that refinement, while Gold serves the resulting business metrics.
explanations.d:
A dashboard query over aggregated data is the documented downstream use of Gold tables.

Additional context:
Gold is optimized for consumers such as dashboards and reports. Querying its stored aggregates avoids rebuilding the same business result for every reader.
explanations.e:
Raw streaming ingestion lands in Bronze, rather than using a business-ready Gold table as its source.

Additional context:
Bronze preserves raw source fidelity and historical landing data. The ingestion job does not need a Gold aggregate as its raw source.

references.section: Power analytics with the gold layer

examTip: Match the layer to what the consumer needs: raw ingestion, cleansing, or reporting.

text:
A dataset has been defined using Delta Live Tables and includes an expectations clause:
CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2020-01-01') ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is
processed?

choices.text:
Records that violate the expectation are dropped
from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in
the event log.

Records that violate the expectation cause the
job to fail.

Records that violate the expectation are dropped
from the target dataset and loaded into a
quarantine table.

Records that violate the expectation are added to
the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the
event log.

Records that violate the expectation are added to
the target dataset and flagged as invalid in a field
added to the target dataset.

originalKeyText:
b) Records that violate the
expectation cause the job
to fail.

explanations.a:
Dropping invalid rows is the DROP ROW action, not the FAIL UPDATE action used here.

Additional context:
DROP ROW is the rule to discard bad rows while continuing a supported update. The source explicitly chooses a different violation action.
explanations.b:
FAIL UPDATE stops the affected flow when the expectation is violated. In this question’s update context, the processing fails; unrelated parallel flows need not stop.

Additional context:
The action applies to the affected flow/update and rolls back the failed table update. Do not generalize it to an unconditional stop of every unrelated parallel flow.
explanations.c:
Quarantine requires a separately implemented routing pattern; FAIL UPDATE does not create a quarantine table.

Additional context:
Quarantine requires defining where valid and invalid records are routed. It is not a side effect automatically added by this expectation.
explanations.d:
Keeping invalid rows and recording metrics corresponds to retaining invalid records, not FAIL UPDATE.

Additional context:
Retaining bad rows with metrics is warning/retain behavior. FAIL UPDATE instead prevents the affected update from committing successfully.
explanations.e:
This expectation does not add a per-row flag column; its configured violation action is to fail the update.

Additional context:
A per-row flag requires an explicit derived field or other application logic. The declared rule only defines validation and its failure action.

references.title: Manage data quality with pipeline expectations
references.section: Action on invalid record — Fail on invalid records
references.support: ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE fails the affected flow update rather than silently retaining or dropping invalid rows.

keyConcept: ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE fails the affected flow update rather than silently retaining or dropping invalid rows.
examTip: Read the violation action literally: fail, drop, and retain have different outcomes.
analysis: ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE fails the affected flow update rather than silently retaining or dropping invalid rows.

text:
Which of the following statements regarding the relationship between Silver tables and Bronze tables is
always true?

choices.text:
Silver tables contain a less refined, less clean view
of data than Bronze data.

Silver tables contain aggregates while Bronze
data is unaggregated.

Silver tables contain more data than Bronze
tables.

Silver tables contain a more refined and cleaner
view of data than Bronze tables.
Silver tables contain less data than Bronze tables.

originalKeyText:
d) Silver tables contain a
more refined and cleaner
view of data than Bronze
tables.

explanations.a:
Silver improves data quality; it is not defined as less refined than Bronze.

Additional context:
Bronze preserves raw fidelity; Silver applies validation and cleaning. Reversing that direction contradicts the documented design.
explanations.b:
Some Silver aggregates are possible, but aggregation is not always present; Gold is the typical reporting aggregate layer.

Additional context:
Some aggregates can be useful in Silver, but they are not mandatory for every Silver table. An always-true answer must describe the quality role instead.
explanations.c:
Joins, deduplication, filtering, and transformations can change row counts in either direction; more data is not guaranteed.

Additional context:
Joins can increase row counts while filtering/deduplication can reduce them. Layer names do not impose a guaranteed cardinality relation.
explanations.d:
A cleaner and more refined representation is the documented quality distinction between Silver and Bronze.

Additional context:
Validated, cleaned representations are Silver’s documented role. That quality distinction holds independently of a particular table’s row count.
explanations.e:
Cleaning may reduce rows, but Silver is not guaranteed to have fewer rows; row count is not the layer’s definition.

Additional context:
Fewer records can be a consequence of cleanup, not a defining law. A valid Silver model might join or enrich data without a smaller cardinality.

references.support: Silver contains validated and cleaned data derived from raw Bronze inputs.

keyConcept: Silver contains validated and cleaned data derived from raw Bronze inputs.
examTip: Layer definitions describe data quality, not a guaranteed increase or decrease in row count.
analysis: Silver contains validated and cleaned data derived from raw Bronze inputs.

text:
Which of the following describes when to use the CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE (formerly CREATE
INCREMENTAL LIVE TABLE) syntax over the CREATE LIVE TABLE syntax when creating Delta Live Tables (DLT)
tables using SQL?

when the subsequent step in the DLT pipeline is
static.

A data engineer is designing a data pipeline. The source system generates files in a shared directory that is

The data engineer needs to identify which files are new since the previous run in the pipeline, and set up the

Delta Lake
Databricks SQL
Data Explorer
Auto Loader

text:
A data engineer is running code in a Databricks Repo that is cloned from a central Git repository. A
colleague of the data engineer informs them that changes have been made and synced to the central
Git repository. The data engineer now needs to sync their Databricks Repo to get the changes from
the central Git repository.
Which of the following Git operations does the data engineer need to run to accomplish this task?

choices.text: Merge
Push
Pull
Commit
Clone

originalKeyText: c) Pull

explanations.a:
Merge combines branches but does not itself fetch the latest remote changes into this checkout.

Additional context:
Merge is appropriate when combining branch histories. It is not by itself the remote update operation asked for here.
explanations.b:
Push sends local commits to the remote, the opposite direction from the requested synchronization.

Additional context:
Push is appropriate after creating local commits that should be published. The colleague’s changes are already remote, so the direction is opposite.
explanations.c:
The documented Pull operation updates notebooks and files from the central remote repository.

Additional context:
The remote-to-local direction is the decisive clue. Resolve conflicts if local edits overlap incoming changes.
explanations.d:
Commit records local changes and does not retrieve a colleague’s remote commits.

Additional context:
Commit saves a chosen local change set in branch history. It does not retrieve another user’s new remote work.
explanations.e:
Clone creates a new working copy; the engineer already has a repo that needs updating.

Additional context:
Clone initializes a new working copy. Updating this existing working copy should not require making another clone.

text:
A data engineer is attempting to drop a Spark SQL table my_table and runs the following command:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS my_table;
After running this command, the engineer notices that the data files and metadata files have been deleted
from the file system.
Which of the following describes why all of these files were deleted?

choices.text: The table was managed
The table's data was smaller than 10 GB
The table's data was larger than 10 GB
The table was external
The table did not have a location

originalKeyText: a) The table was managed

explanations.a: Managed table lifecycle is the listed reason metadata and associated data are subject to deletion on DROP. Unity Catalog’s documented recovery/purge delay is an important modern caveat.
explanations.b: There is no small-table 10-GB rule deciding whether DROP deletes files. Table type and lifecycle semantics matter instead.
explanations.c: A large table is not exempt from the managed lifecycle, nor is size the explanation for it. The operation is not governed by this cutoff.
explanations.d: External tables are the opposite case: DROP removes the catalog definition while preserving externally managed files. It does not match the reported data deletion.
explanations.e: Even a managed table with no explicit LOCATION still has platform-managed storage. Lack of a typed location clause is not independently the lifecycle rule.

references.title: DROP TABLE
references.section: DROP TABLE; Managed-table recovery and purge

examTip: Managed versus external determines ownership of deletion; file size does not.

text:
A data engineer has been given a new record of data:
id STRING = 'a1'
rank INTEGER = 6
rating FLOAT = 9.4
Which of the following SQL commands can be used to append the new record to an existing Delta table
my_table?

choices.text: INSERT INTO my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
my_table UNION VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
INSERT VALUES ( 'a1' , 6, 9.4) INTO my_table
UPDATE my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
UPDATE VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4) my_table

originalKeyText:
a) INSERT INTO my_table
VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)

explanations.a:
INSERT INTO my_table VALUES supplies the target table followed by the literal row, appending the requested record.

Additional context:
INTO appends rather than replacing the table. Column ordering and compatible types must still match the target definition when no column list is given.
explanations.b:
A UNION combines query results; this fragment is not an INSERT and does not persist a new row to my_table.

Additional context:
UNION is a query-result set operation, not a persistence command by itself. A complete INSERT could consume a query, but that is not the printed fragment.
explanations.c:
The documented syntax places INTO and the target table before the VALUES query, not after the values.

Additional context:
The target must be specified before the inserted query/VALUES clause. SQL keyword order is part of validating the complete DML statement.
explanations.d:
UPDATE modifies existing rows and uses SET assignments; UPDATE ... VALUES is not the append syntax.

Additional context:
UPDATE uses SET and a predicate to change existing records. Adding a new literal record requires INSERT rather than this malformed UPDATE.
explanations.e:
This reverses the required target and assignment structure and is not a supported INSERT statement.

Additional context:
Both the verb and clause ordering are wrong for appending a record. Correct literal values do not make an invalid DML statement executable.

examTip: Distinguish appending a new record from updating existing rows.
analysis: INSERT INTO appends rows, with VALUES supplying a new literal row.

text:
A data engineer has realized that the data files associated with a Delta table are incredibly small. They want
to compact the small files to form larger files to improve performance.
Which of the following keywords can be used to compact the small files?

choices.text: REDUCE
OPTIMIZE
COMPACTION
REPARTITION
VACUUM

originalKeyText: b) OPTIMIZE

explanations.a:
REDUCE is not the documented Delta SQL command for compaction.

Additional context:
The operation name must be the supported Delta command. A plausible synonym is not a SQL keyword for table compaction.
explanations.b:
OPTIMIZE performs file compaction, combining small data files to improve the table’s physical layout.

Additional context:
Compaction changes physical layout without changing the logical records returned. It is different from deleting unreferenced historical files.
explanations.c:
Compaction describes the operation, but COMPACTION is not the documented SQL command to invoke it.

Additional context:
Use the documented OPTIMIZE spelling rather than a descriptive noun. The distinction matters when executing table maintenance SQL.
explanations.d:
Repartitioning a DataFrame is not the Delta table maintenance command requested, and by itself does not rewrite the existing table files.

Additional context:
A repartitioned DataFrame would still need a deliberate write strategy to affect table files. It is not the single maintenance keyword requested.
explanations.e:
VACUUM removes unreferenced files older than retention; it does not combine active small files into larger ones.

Additional context:
VACUUM is appropriate for reclaiming eligible stale files after retention. It is not a rewrite that consolidates current small data files.

references.support: OPTIMIZE compacts small data files while preserving logical table contents.

CSV
Parquet
JSON

A proprietary, optimized format specific to
Databricks

originalKeyText: c) Parquet

explanations.a:
Delta names the table protocol and transaction layer; its primary data files are Parquet.

Additional context:
A format name can refer to a table protocol rather than its physical row-file encoding. Delta’s protocol adds transaction semantics around Parquet data.
explanations.b:

Additional context:
The file-based transaction log complements Parquet rather than replacing it with a proprietary encoding. That is why the primary data-file answer is Parquet.
explanations.d:
JSON is used in parts of transaction metadata, not as the primary table data-file format.

Additional context:
JSON log records describe transaction actions and metadata. They should not be confused with the main files storing table rows.
explanations.e:
Delta Lake is open source and uses Parquet; its table data is not a proprietary Databricks-only file format.

Additional context:

(SLA) that demands minimal runtime errors and high availability for its data processing
pipelines. The data engineer wants to avoid the operational overhead of managing and tuning
clusters.

monitored by the user.

Implement a hybrid approach with scheduled
batch jobs on custom cloud VMs.

optimized by in-house IT staff.

explanations.a: User-managed autoscaling still requires compute configuration and monitoring. It does not remove the operational burden the question explicitly wants to avoid.
explanations.b: Custom VMs add infrastructure lifecycle and orchestration responsibilities. That is the opposite of the desired abstraction.
explanations.c: A manually tuned dedicated cluster maintains the same staffing and tuning burden. It does not satisfy the minimal management requirement.

text:
A data engineering project involves processing large batches of data on a daily schedule using
ETL. The jobs are resource-intensive and vary in size, requiring a scalable, cost-efficient
compute solution that can automatically scale based on the workload.
Which compute approach will satisfy the needs described?

choices.text: Job Cluster
Dedicated Cluster
All-Purpose Cluster
Databricks SQL Serverless

originalKeyText: a) Job Cluster

explanations.a: Jobs compute is intended for automated scheduled workloads and can scale resources through supported cluster settings. Its lifecycle avoids keeping an interactive cluster idle between runs.
explanations.b: Dedicated describes an access mode or a reserved cluster concept, not necessarily the job-scoped scalable lifecycle requested. It does not by itself establish the desired schedule/termination behavior.
explanations.c: All-purpose compute serves interactive work and may remain running between jobs. It is not the most direct job-scoped lifecycle among these choices.
explanations.d: A serverless SQL warehouse executes supported SQL analytics tasks. The scenario describes general batch ETL and does not restrict the workload to warehouse-compatible SQL.

text:
A data engineer is maintaining a data pipeline. Upon data ingestion, the data engineer notices
that the source data is starting to have a lower level of quality. The data engineer would like to
automate the process of monitoring the quality level.
Which of the following tools can the data engineer use to solve this problem?

choices.text: Auto Loader
Unity Catalog
Delta Lake
Delta Live Tables

originalKeyText: d) Delta Live Tables

explanations.a: Auto Loader ingests newly arriving files and manages schema evolution. It is not the expectation framework for arbitrary business-quality checks across transformed tables.
explanations.b: Unity Catalog controls governance and access to data objects. Governance alone does not define the source record quality rules described here.
explanations.c: Delta Lake provides transactional table storage and schema enforcement. The named managed-pipeline feature for richer expectation metrics is DLT/Lakeflow.
explanations.d: DLT/Lakeflow expectations evaluate Boolean quality constraints and report retained or dropped invalid rows. They are directly intended for automated pipeline data quality monitoring.

region

explanations.a: The cited reference says in-region sharing does not incur egress cost under the described model. It is not the cross-region/cross-cloud case singled out by the question.

explanations.c: A VPN in one data center is not what the sharing reference identifies as cross-region egress. Network architecture may have its own costs but does not establish this data-sharing charge.

text:
An organization has data stored across multiple external systems, including MySQL, Amazon
Redshift, and Google BigQuery. The data engineer wants to perform analytics without ingesting
directly into Databricks, ensuring unified governance and minimizing data duplication.
Which feature of Databricks enables querying these external data sources while maintaining
centralized governance?

choices.text: Delta Lake
Lakehouse Federation
MLflow
Databricks Connect

originalKeyText: b) Lakehouse Federation

explanations.a: Delta Lake supplies transactional storage for tables. It does not by itself create governed query federation over MySQL, Redshift, and BigQuery.
explanations.b: Lakehouse Federation provides governed foreign catalogs and query pushdown for supported sources. It matches the goal of minimizing ingestion and duplication.
explanations.c: MLflow manages machine-learning experiments and model lifecycle. It is not the external relational query federation feature.
explanations.d: Databricks Connect submits Spark work from a local client to Databricks compute. It is not itself the centralized governance/federation layer over those databases.

references.title: Connect to external databases and catalogs
references.section: Lakehouse Federation; Query federation
references.support: Lakehouse Federation queries supported external databases through Unity Catalog foreign catalogs without first replicating all data into local tables. Source connectivity, permissions, and supported database types remain prerequisites.

analysis: Lakehouse Federation queries supported external databases through Unity Catalog foreign catalogs without first replicating all data into local tables. Source connectivity, permissions, and supported database types remain prerequisites.
keyConcept: Lakehouse Federation queries supported external databases through Unity Catalog foreign catalogs without first replicating all data into local tables. Source connectivity, permissions, and supported database types remain prerequisites.
examTip: Query external systems in place with foreign catalogs; use ingestion when a managed local copy is needed.

text:
An organization needs to share a dataset stored in its Databricks Unity Catalog with an external
partner who uses a different data platform that is not Databricks. The goal is to maintain data
security and ensure the partner can access the data efficiently.
Which method should the data engineer use to securely share the dataset with the external
partner?

choices.text:
Using Delta Sharing with the open sharing
protocol
Exporting data as CSV files and emailing them
Using a third-party API to access the Delta table
Databricks-to-Databricks Sharing

originalKeyText:
a) Using Delta Sharing with
the open sharing protocol

explanations.a: The open protocol is designed to share governed assets with recipients on other platforms. Appropriate recipient authentication and share grants control access.
explanations.b: Emailing CSV copies loses the governed live-share workflow and requires separate file security/lifecycle controls. It is not the secure sharing mechanism requested.
explanations.c: A third-party API is an unspecified custom solution with no defined governance or authentication here. The native open sharing protocol already meets the interoperability requirement.
explanations.d: Databricks-to-Databricks sharing expects the corresponding Databricks recipient environment. The partner in this question explicitly uses a different platform.

text:
A data engineer is configuring Unity Catalog in Databricks and needs to assign a role to a user
who should have the ability to grant and revoke privileges on various data objects within a
specific schema, but should not have read/write access over the schema or its objects.
Which role should the data engineer assign to this user?

choices.text: Table Owner
Catalog Owner
Schema Owner
USE catalog/schema privilege on the schema

originalKeyText: c) Schema Owner

explanations.a: A table owner has all privileges on that table and scope limited to that object. It is not the requested schema-wide delegation without automatic table access.
explanations.b: A catalog owner has broader administrative scope than one schema. It exceeds the stated delegation boundary.
explanations.c: A schema owner can manage privileges on contained objects, making C the source’s likely intended role. Ownership is broader than MANAGE and can allow self-granting child-table access, so it is not strict separation from data access.
explanations.d: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are namespace access prerequisites. They do not grant authority to grant or revoke privileges for other users.

text:
A data engineer at a company that uses Databricks with Unity Catalog needs to share a
collection of tables with an external partner who also uses a Databricks workspace enabled for
Unity Catalog. The data engineer decides to use Delta Sharing to accomplish this.
What is the first piece of information the data engineer should request from the external partner
to set up Delta Sharing?

choices.text: The IP address of their Databricks workspace
The name of their Databricks cluster

The sharing identifier of their Unity Catalog
metastore
Their Databricks account password

originalKeyText:
c) The sharing identifier of
their Unity Catalog
metastore

explanations.a: A workspace IP address is not the recipient’s Unity Catalog sharing identity. Network addresses do not define the share recipient object.
explanations.b: Cluster names can change and do not identify the recipient metastore. Sharing is governed at the catalog/metastore level rather than tied to a chosen cluster name.
explanations.c: The sharing identifier is the documented identifier for the recipient metastore. It lets the provider create the appropriate Databricks recipient relationship.
explanations.d: A password is neither needed nor appropriate for setting up a provider-to-recipient share. Sharing identity and grants avoid using another organization’s login credentials.

references.section: Databricks-to-Databricks sharing workflow

policies or manually applied row filters and column masks to protect sensitive data across their catalog.
Why should the team use ABAC policies instead of manually applied row filters and column masks?

choices.text:
ABAC policies use governed tags to dynamically
match tables and columns, so a single policy
defined on a catalog automatically applies to all
current and future tables within that catalog
without per-table configuration.

ABAC policies allow row filters and column masks
to be written in Python and Scala directly,
whereas manually applied filters and masks can
only use SQL user-defined functions.

ABAC policies can be applied to views and
materialized views in addition to tables, whereas
manually applied row filters and column masks
can only be applied to tables.

ABAC policies support applying multiple distinct
row filters to the same table for a single user at
query time, whereas manually applied row filters

originalKeyText:
a) ABAC policies use
governed tags to
dynamically match tables
and columns, so a single
policy defined on a catalog
automatically applies to all
current and future tables
within that catalog without
per-table configuration.

explanations.a: A describes dynamically matching governed tags and centrally scoped policies. Read all current/future tables as the matching objects within the policy scope, not every untagged table.

text:
A data engineer is onboarding a new bronze ingestion pipeline in Databricks with Unity Catalog. The team
wants Databricks to handle storage layout, apply platform optimizations over time, and simplify lifecycle
management so that when a table is dropped, its underlying data is also cleaned up according to
Databricks-managed retention policies.
Which table type should the data engineer create for these ingestion tables?

choices.text:
Managed tables so that Unity Catalog manages
both metadata and underlying data lifecycle.

External tables with a LOCATION pointing to an
external volume for full control of file layout.

Foreign tables federated from an external catalog
to delegate optimization to the source system

Temporary views over files to avoid table-level
governance and lifecycle coupling.

originalKeyText:
a) Managed tables so that
Unity Catalog manages
both metadata and
underlying data lifecycle.

explanations.a: A matches managed metadata and data lifecycle, with deletion governed by the platform’s retention/recovery rules. It fits the explicit operational goal.
explanations.b: External tables keep file ownership/lifecycle external to the catalog definition. Dropping their metadata does not request the managed cleanup behavior.
explanations.c: Foreign tables reference externally governed source systems and do not become local managed ingestion storage merely through federation. They do not satisfy platform-managed local lifecycle.
explanations.d: A temporary view is nonmaterialized and session-scoped. It does not provide the durable governed Bronze storage and data lifecycle requested.

references.title: Unity Catalog managed tables for Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg
references.section: Managed table lifecycle; DROP TABLE
references.support: Unity Catalog managed tables delegate both metadata and underlying data lifecycle to Databricks, including supported platform optimization and managed deletion/recovery behavior. External tables retain a separately managed file lifecycle.

references.title: DROP TABLE
references.section: Managed table lifecycle; DROP TABLE
references.support: Unity Catalog managed tables delegate both metadata and underlying data lifecycle to Databricks, including supported platform optimization and managed deletion/recovery behavior. External tables retain a separately managed file lifecycle.

analysis: Unity Catalog managed tables delegate both metadata and underlying data lifecycle to Databricks, including supported platform optimization and managed deletion/recovery behavior. External tables retain a separately managed file lifecycle.
keyConcept: Unity Catalog managed tables delegate both metadata and underlying data lifecycle to Databricks, including supported platform optimization and managed deletion/recovery behavior. External tables retain a separately managed file lifecycle.
examTip: Choose managed when the platform should own placement, optimization, and eventual cleanup.

text:
A data engineer is decommissioning a sandbox schema in Unity Catalog. Some tables are ephemeral staging
outputs that can be safety removed entirely, but a few tables point at shared cloud storage used by
downstream jobs outside Databricks. The engineer must avoid deleting any shared files when cleaning up
catalog objects.
How does Unity Catalog behave when dropping Managed vs External tables?

choices.text:
DROP all tables; Databricks will only remove
metadata for both managed and external tables.

DROP managed tables that are ephemeral and
DROP external tables; files for both remain for 7
days.

DROP managed staging tables to remove data
and metadata, and DROP external tables to
remove only metadata

DROP external tables first to delete their files,
then DROP managed tables to keep their files for
recovery.

originalKeyText:
c) DROP managed staging
tables to remove data and
metadata, and DROP
external tables to remove
only metadata

explanations.a: Managed tables are not permanently metadata-only deletion cases. Their underlying data is subject to platform lifecycle cleanup.
explanations.b: External data is not simply held for seven days and then deleted by DROP. The catalog drop leaves externally managed files in place.
explanations.c: C correctly distinguishes managed data/metadata lifecycle from external metadata-only removal. Apply the documented recovery/purge delay rather than assuming instantaneous managed deletion.
explanations.d: This reverses the documented behaviors. External DROP does not delete the shared files, while managed lifecycle can eventually remove data.

references.title: DROP TABLE
references.section: External tables; Managed recovery and purge
references.support: Dropping external tables removes catalog metadata without deleting their shared files. Managed staging data is subject to managed deletion, which can be delayed by Unity Catalog recovery and purge policies.

analysis: Dropping external tables removes catalog metadata without deleting their shared files. Managed staging data is subject to managed deletion, which can be delayed by Unity Catalog recovery and purge policies.
keyConcept: Dropping external tables removes catalog metadata without deleting their shared files. Managed staging data is subject to managed deletion, which can be delayed by Unity Catalog recovery and purge policies.
examTip: A table disappearing from the catalog does not mean every physical file is immediately deleted.

text:
A data engineer wants to delegate day-to-day permission management for the schema main marketing to
the mkt-admins group, without making them workspace admins. They should be able to grant and revoke
privileges for other users on objects within that schema.
Which approach aligns with UC’s ownership and privilege model?

choices.text:
Grant MANAGE permissions on the metastore to
mkt-admins, which allows managing privileges for
all schemas and tables globally.

Make mkt-admins a workspace-level admins
group, then SELECT on main.marketing to allow
privilege delegation.

Transfer ownership of the schema main.marketing
to mkt-admins; owners can manage privileges on
the schema and its contained objects.

Grant USE SCHEMA on main.marketing and
MODIFY on all tables to mkt-admins, which
enables managing grants within the schema.

originalKeyText:
c) Transfer ownership of the
schema main.marketing to
mkt-admins; owners can
manage privileges on the
schema and its contained
objects.

explanations.a: A metastore-wide MANAGE grant is not the narrowly scoped schema ownership model requested and is not expressed as a supported universal global privilege here. It would exceed the intended scope.
explanations.b: Making the group workspace admins directly contradicts the requirement. SELECT alone also does not confer grant/revoke authority.
explanations.c: A schema owner can manage privileges on the schema and its contained objects. Transferring schema ownership to the intended group implements that delegation model.
explanations.d: USE SCHEMA and MODIFY permit namespace access and data changes, not management of other users’ grants. Data privileges do not imply ownership administration.
