text:
A data engineer needs to access the view created by the sales team, using a shared cluster. The data
engineer has been provided usage permissions on the catalog and schema. In order to access the view
created by sales team. What are the minimum permissions the data engineer would require in addition?

choices.text:
Needs SELECT permission on the VIEW and the
underlying TABLE.
Needs SELECT permission only on the VIEW
Needs ALL PRIVILEGES on the VIEW
Needs ALL PRIVILEGES at the SCHEMA level

originalKeyText:
b) Needs SELECT permission
only on the VIEW

explanations.a: Requiring the caller to read the underlying table is broader than necessary in the supported standard/shared view model. It can defeat a view-based security boundary.
explanations.b: SELECT on the view, with the already supplied namespace usage and valid owner dependencies, is the least-privilege additional grant in this context. The compute/access-mode assumption is important.
explanations.c: ALL PRIVILEGES grants more than the view query capability requested. SELECT is sufficient under the stated supported access model.
explanations.d: Schema-wide ALL privileges greatly exceeds access to one view. It is not a minimum additional grant.

text:
dentify the impact of ON VIOLATION DROP ROW and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE for a constraint violation. A
data engineer has created an ETL pipeline using Delta Live table to manage their company travel
reimbursement detail, they want to ensure that the if the location details has not been provided by the
employee, the pipeline needs to be terminated. How can the scenario be implemented?

choices.text:
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location =
NULL)

CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location !=
NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE

CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location !=
NULL) ON DROP ROW

CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location !=
NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL

originalKeyText:
b) CONSTRAINT
valid_location EXPECT
(location != NULL) ON
VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE

explanations.a: location = NULL is not a valid null-presence test and no failure action is specified. It does not express the desired valid-location constraint.
explanations.b: FAIL UPDATE is the right action, but location != NULL evaluates to unknown rather than true for non-null values. It would not implement the intended rule that valid locations pass.
explanations.c: The predicate has the same NULL-comparison defect and ON DROP ROW is not the required FAIL UPDATE action. Dropping rows also does not terminate the update.
explanations.d: ON VIOLATION FAIL is not the documented FAIL UPDATE syntax, and the predicate still compares with NULL incorrectly. Both issues prevent the requested behavior.

text:
In a healthcare provider organization using Delta Lake to store electronic health records (EHRs), a data
analyst needs to analyze a snapshot of the patient_records table from two weeks ago before some recent
data corrections were applied. What approach should the Data Engineer take to allow the analyst to query
that specific prior version?

choices.text:
Truncate the table to remove all data, then reload
the data from two weeks ago into the truncated
table for the analyst to query.

Identify the version number corresponding to two
weeks ago from the Delta transaction log, share
that version number with the analyst to query
using VERSION AS OF syntax, or export that
version to a new Delta table for the analyst to
query.

Restore the table to the version from two weeks
ago using the RESTORE command, and have the
analyst query the restored table.

Use the VACUUM command to remove all versions
of the table older than two weeks, then the
analyst can query the remaining version

originalKeyText:
b) Identify the version
number corresponding to
two weeks ago from the
Delta transaction log,
share that version number
with the analyst to query
using VERSION AS OF
syntax, or export that
version to a new Delta

explanations.a: Truncating and reloading destroys or changes the current table state just to support an analysis. It is unnecessary and risky when a retained snapshot can be read directly.
explanations.b: B selects the historical version through VERSION AS OF or materializes that snapshot separately. It satisfies the analysis need without rolling back the live table, subject to retention.
explanations.c: RESTORE makes an old snapshot the current table version. That affects other consumers and is not required merely to let one analyst inspect history.
explanations.d: VACUUM deletes unreferenced data files and can remove time-travel capability. It does not choose a readable prior version for the analyst.

references.section: Query an older snapshot; Retention limitations
references.support: Use a retained historical table version or timestamp for non-destructive analysis. Two-week-old data files are not guaranteed by the default seven-day VACUUM retention; verify that the required files and log history still exist.

examTip: Time travel is a read of history; RESTORE changes the current table.

text:
A dataset has been defined using Delta Live Tables and includes an expectations clause:
CONSTRAINT valid timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > ‘2020-01 01’) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is
processed?

choices.text:
Records that violate the expectation cause the
job to fail.

Records that violate the expectation are added to
the target dataset and flagged as invalid in a field
added to the target dataset.

Records that violate the expectation are dropped
from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in
the event log.

Records that violate the expectation are added to
the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the
event log.

originalKeyText:
c) Records that violate the
expectation are dropped
from the target dataset
and recorded as invalid in
the event log.

explanations.a: Failing the flow is the behavior of FAIL UPDATE, not DROP ROW. A dropped-record rule can complete successfully with fewer output rows.
explanations.b: DROP ROW does not retain bad records or automatically add an invalid flag field. It removes them before target output.
explanations.c: C describes dropping violating rows and reporting the invalid/dropped counts. This is the documented DROP ROW behavior.
explanations.d: Retaining invalid records while recording metrics corresponds to the default warning/retain action. It contradicts the explicit DROP ROW instruction.

analysis: ON VIOLATION DROP ROW removes invalid records while allowing a supported flow update to continue and records dropped counts in quality metrics. The source’s typographic identifier/date formatting should not be copied as a validated standalone SQL statement.

examTip: DROP ROW is not FAIL UPDATE and does not automatically create a quarantine table or a flag column.

text:
A data engineer has three tables in a Delta Live Tables (DLT) pipeline. They have configured the pipeline to
drop invalid records at each table. They notice that some data is being dropped due to quality concerns at
some point in the DLT pipeline. They would like to determine at which table in their pipeline the data is being
dropped. Which approach can the data engineer take to identify the table that is dropping the records?

choices.text:
They can set up separate expectations for each
table when developing their DLT pipeline.

They can navigate to the DLT pipeline page, click
on the “Error” button, and review the present
errors.

They can set up DLT to notify them via email
when records are dropped.

They can navigate to the DLT pipeline page, click
on each table, and view the data quality
statistics.

originalKeyText:
d) They can navigate to the
DLT pipeline page, click on
each table, and view the
data quality statistics.

explanations.a: Expectations define the quality rules, but the prompt already says rules are dropping records. Adding more rules is not the direct way to inspect the existing losses.
explanations.b: Dropped invalid rows do not necessarily fail the flow. Looking only for error messages can miss successful updates that intentionally discard records.
explanations.c: A notification can report an event but does not replace examining per-table quality statistics. The option does not identify which existing expectation dropped the rows.
explanations.d: Opening each pipeline dataset and its quality metrics reveals the counts of passed and dropped records. This is the documented inspection path for the configured drop behavior.

references.section: Expectation tracking metrics
references.support: The pipeline UI exposes expectation metrics for dataset updates using warn or drop actions. Inspecting each dataset’s dropped-record counts identifies where quality rules discard rows.

text:
A new data engineering team team has been assigned to an ELT project. The new data engineering team will
need full privileges on the database customers to fully manage the project.
Which of the following commands can be used to grant full permissions on the database to the new data
engineering team?

GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE team TO
customers;

GRANT SELECT PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE
customers TO teams;

What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is

Records that violate the expectation are dropped
from the target dataset and loaded into a
quarantine table.

Records that violate the expectation cause the

Records that violate the expectation are dropped

explanations.a: A quarantine table must be defined through a separate routing design. DROP ROW alone does not create and populate one.
explanations.b: FAIL UPDATE is the action that stops the affected update. DROP ROW instead discards bad records while processing may continue.
explanations.c: C matches the documented drop behavior and quality metrics. Invalid rows are not written to the target dataset.

text:
A Databricks Job with four sequential tasks is executed. The job failed at Task 3. After the root cause is fixed,
the data engineer needs to complete the workflow without re-running the successful Tasks 1 and 2.
Which action in the Job Run details page allows the engineer to resume execution from the point of failure?

choices.text: Repair run
Reset job
Clone task
Run now

originalKeyText: a) Repair run

explanations.a: Repair run selects the failed work and dependents in the existing run’s recovery workflow. It avoids repeating successful earlier tasks unnecessarily.
explanations.b: Reset job is not the run recovery action documented for this purpose. Resetting resource configuration is different from selecting failed task executions.
explanations.c: Cloning a task changes the job definition and does not resume the failed execution. It can create duplicate work rather than repairing the recorded run.
explanations.d: Run now starts a fresh execution of the job. It does not inherently skip the already successful first two tasks of the failed run.

keyConcept: Repair run can rerun failed Task 3 and the required downstream portion while retaining successful Tasks 1 and 2. The multi-task condition is satisfied in this four-task job.
examTip: Repair is for a recorded failed run; Run now starts a new run.

text:
A data engineering team runs multiple daily batch jobs. The team needs to run the jobs on a fixed overnight

Classic all-purpose compute
Serverless jobs compute
Classic jobs compute

originalKeyText: c) Serverless jobs compute

explanations.a: SQL warehouses are for supported SQL analytics tasks, not an automatic replacement for every general ETL job. The task language and execution interface still matter.
explanations.b: Classic all-purpose compute can remain idle between overnight jobs and requires cluster lifecycle management. It is not the lowest operational overhead option here.
explanations.c: Serverless jobs compute directly targets managed provisioning and job execution without manually maintaining a cluster. It best matches the stated overhead and idle-cost goals among the choices.
explanations.d: Classic jobs compute also avoids much idle cost, but the user still manages cluster configurations and sizing choices. Serverless more directly meets the minimal operational overhead requirement.

Continuous trigger

explanations.b: A file-arrival trigger watches storage paths, not the committed update state of a Unity Catalog table. It is a different event boundary.
explanations.c: A scheduled trigger runs according to time, whether or not the Bronze table changed. It does not directly express reacting to the table update.

text:
A data engineer triggers a scheduled job but finds that the new run was not executed. The run history shows
the run was skipped with a concurrency related queue message.
Which configuration should the engineer investigate?

The task-level timeout_seconds configuration

The job-level max_concurrent_runs setting and
whether queueing is enabled

The cluster spot-instance availability in the cloud
provider

c) The job-level
max_concurrent_runs
setting and whether
queueing is enabled

explanations.b: A task timeout acts after a task is running too long. It is not the job-level policy that skips an overlapping triggered run.
explanations.c: Check max_concurrent_runs and whether queueing is enabled. These govern the observed overlapping-run admission behavior.

Task C depends on Task A (All done) and Task B

Task C depends on Task A (Success) with Task B
listed as a negative dependency.

Task C uses two dependency chains: Task A with
All succeeded, Task B with at least one failed.

Create a Python task that checks

text:
A data engineering team runs nightly batch ETL pipelines that transform large volumes of data stored in

An all-purpose compute cluster configured with
autoscaling.

A Databricks SQL warehouse configured for
serverless execution.

A single-node compute cluster configured

A job compute cluster triggered by a scheduled
workflow.

d) A job compute cluster
triggered by a scheduled
workflow.

explanations.b: A serverless SQL warehouse is appropriate for warehouse-supported SQL tasks. The question does not state that these general ETL pipelines are restricted to SQL warehouse execution.
explanations.c: A fixed single-node cluster cannot provide the requested automatic distributed scaling. It may also lack resources for the stated large-volume transformations.
explanations.d: A scheduled job compute cluster can scale under its configuration and terminate after the job. That matches periodic batch work and avoiding idle compute between executions.

text:
A notebook task check_volume calculates a daily data volume and writes it to a Lakeflow Jobs taskValue
named record_count. If the count is greater than 1 million, the job should run high volumepipeline; otherwise,
it should run normal_pipeline.
Which control-flow feature should be used?

choices.text:
Add an I£/else condition task that reads the
record_count task value and routes to different
downstream tasks.

Use a For each task over the record_count and
stop when it is below the threshold.

Configure additional retries for check_volume
until the count exceeds the threshold.

Configure Run if conditions based purely on task
status.

originalKeyText:
a) Add an I£/else condition
task that reads the
record_count task value
and routes to different
downstream tasks.

explanations.a: A reads the task value in the condition operand and compares it to the threshold. The true and false branches can select high-volume versus normal processing.
explanations.b: For each repeats a nested task over an array, not a numeric threshold branch. A scalar record count is not an iteration plan.
explanations.c: Retries repeat work after failure and do not implement a normal business branch. Repeating until volume changes is not the required deterministic workflow.
explanations.d: Run-if conditions inspect dependency result status rather than the numeric record_count. Both upstream runs could succeed with different counts, so status alone is insufficient.

references.title: Add branching logic to a job with the If/else task
references.section: Configure an If/else task; Task values
references.support: An If/else task compares the published record_count task value with 1000000 and routes downstream tasks on its true/false result. Run-if status policies do not inspect the numeric count.

keyConcept: An If/else task compares the published record_count task value with 1000000 and routes downstream tasks on its true/false result. Run-if status policies do not inspect the numeric count.
examTip: Branch on a business metric with If/else; branch on success/failure with run-if policies.

text:
A data engineer is designing a Databricks Job that includes a Notebook task for data cleansing and a SQL
Query task for generating a summary report. The summary report must only execute after the cleansing
task completes successfully.
How should the dependency be configured in the Lakeflow Jobs task graph?

Select the cleansing task as a 'Run if' dependency
in the summary report task configuration.

Set both tasks to run on the same schedule with
a five-minute start delay for the report.

Configure the cleansing task to use an 'On Failure’
trigger to start the summary report.

Place both tasks in the same notebook and use a
standard Python function call.

originalKeyText:
a) Select the cleansing task
as a 'Run if' dependency in
the summary report task
configuration.

explanations.a: Selecting cleansing as the summary task’s dependency, with All succeeded, makes the report wait for successful cleansing. This directly implements the required order and outcome.
explanations.b: A five-minute delay can expire while cleansing is still running or failed. Independent schedules do not establish a task success condition.
explanations.c: On Failure is the opposite result condition from the requirement. It would attempt to start the summary when cleansing did not succeed.
explanations.d: Combining work into one notebook changes the architecture rather than configuring the stated Notebook and SQL Query task graph. It is unnecessary for a supported dependency edge.

references.title: Configure task dependencies

text:

deploy -> databricks bundle run

text:
A company has a strict 15-minute Service Level Agreement (SLA) for updating its currency exchange
dashboard. The source data arrives in small increments every few minutes. The data engineering team
needs a triggering strategy for their Lakeflow Job that keeps end-to-end latency within the SLA while
minimizing compute cost and DBU consumption.
Which triggering strategy for the Lakeflow Job is the recommended way to meet this 15-minute SLA?

choices.text:
Use a Scheduled trigger set to run every 12
minutes, with the streaming task configured to
use Trigger .AvailableNow.

Use a Scheduled trigger set to run every 1 minute
to ensure the SLA is never at risk.

Use a File Arrival trigger configured to fire every
time a single JSON file lands in the bucket.

Use a Continuous trigger to ensure data is
processed as soon as it arrives.

a) Use a Scheduled trigger
set to run every 12
minutes, with the
streaming task configured
to use Trigger
.AvailableNow.

explanations.b: One-minute scheduling can spend more on repeated starts and still does not guarantee successful end-to-end completion. The claim that the SLA is never at risk is unsupported.
explanations.c: File arrivals can make ingestion event-driven, but actual arrival coalescing, trigger delay, and per-run overhead determine cost. The prompt supplies no evidence that every-file triggering is optimal.
explanations.d: Continuous processing can reduce latency but generally keeps compute active longer. It is not automatically the minimum-cost solution for small increments and a 15-minute target.

text:
A data engineer observes that an ETL job in Databricks has increased its execution time from 5
minutes (baseline) to 12 minutes over the past week. Using the Lakeflow Jobs run history view, the
engineer needs to identify whether the slowdown is consistent or intermittent and determine the
root cause.
Which action should the engineer take to analyze execution time trends against the baseline?

choices.text:
Compare cluster metrics in Lakeflow Jobs run
history to spot resource spikes causing
delays.

Archive old job runs and resets the baseline
counter to ensure accurate comparison of
current performance.

Rerun the job immediately to establish a new
baseline since historical data becomes
irrelevant after seven days.

Increase cluster size automatically whenever
execution time exceeds the previous run's
duration.

originalKeyText:
a) Compare cluster metrics
in Lakeflow Jobs run
history to spot resource
spikes causing delays.

explanations.a: A uses recorded run and resource evidence to investigate the regression. Pair the run-duration trend with detailed task/compute inspection rather than assume every delay is caused by a resource spike.
explanations.b: Archiving old runs removes the evidence needed to compare against the baseline. Resetting a counter does not diagnose the underlying slowdown.
explanations.c: There is no universal rule making seven-day-old run information irrelevant. Rerunning alone cannot determine whether the prior week’s slowdown was consistent.
explanations.d: Automatically increasing cluster size before diagnosis can add cost without fixing skew, I/O, or code regressions. A slower run is evidence to investigate, not proof of undersized hardware.

text:
A data engineering team uses Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles)
to deploy the same codebase across dev, test, and prod environments. The team wants
environment-specific behavior to be applied only through bundle configuration, without modifying
notebooks, job definitions, or deployment logic during promotion.
Which approach applies environment-specific configuration while meeting this requirement?

choices.text:
Use separate Git branches per environment
so each branch can contain environment
specific configuration values.

Define bundle variables and reference them
from bundle resources, then override variable
values per environment using bundle targets.

Parameterize environment-specific values
inside notebooks and set those parameters
when each job run is triggered.

Deploy the same bundle once and edit job
settings in the workspace UI for each
environment after deployment.

originalKeyText:
b) Define bundle variables
and reference them from
bundle resources, then
override variable values
per environment using
bundle targets.

explanations.a:
Separate branches change the codebase during promotion and do not meet the requirement for configuration-only environment behavior.

Additional context:
Branches control source versions, not merely deployment-time values. The scenario explicitly wants the same codebase promoted with configuration-only differences.
explanations.b:
Referencing ${var.name} and overriding variables under bundle targets supplies environment-specific values at deployment without editing resource definitions.

Additional context:
Resource references use ${var.name}, while the selected target supplies its overrides. This is deployment-time configuration rather than a notebook code edit.
explanations.c:
Notebook job parameters are runtime inputs; the requirement is deployment-time environment behavior through bundle configuration.

Additional context:
Job parameters supply runtime values to an execution. They do not automatically replace bundle-level deployment settings for resources.
explanations.d:
Manual workspace edits bypass the versioned bundle configuration and do not make environment behavior reproducible through configuration alone.

Additional context:
Manual edits create drift between the reviewed source configuration and deployed workspace objects. Reproducible promotion should flow through target configuration.

text:
A data engineer configures a Databricks Lakeflow Job for daily customer data processing: + Entry
task: Single notebook loads raw data » Parallel tasks: o SQL query task for cleansing o Notebook
task for feature engineering o Pipeline task for model updates » Exit task: Dashboard refresh (must
run after all parallel tasks complete) + Requirement: Implement this dependency pattern using a
DAG-based task graph
Which task configuration ensures all parallel tasks complete before the dashboard refresh task
runs?

choices.text:
Create separate Lakeflow Jobs for each
parallel task and trigger them sequentially
using external orchestration.

Add the dashboard task as dependent on all
three parallel tasks using fan-in control flow.

Configure the parallel tasks with sequential
dependencies so each task waits for the
previous one to finish.

Set the dashboard task to depend only on
the SQL query task; other tasks run
independently.

originalKeyText:
b) Add the dashboard task
as dependent on all
three parallel tasks using
fan-in control flow.

explanations.a:
Separate externally sequenced jobs do not implement the requested dependency graph inside this Lakeflow Job.

Additional context:
External sequential scheduling discards both the single-job DAG and the requested parallel middle stage. It also adds another orchestration layer.
explanations.b:
Adding all three tasks as dashboard dependencies creates the fan-in graph. Use All succeeded by default, or All done if completion regardless of success is explicitly intended.

Additional context:
The dashboard is the fan-in consumer of all three parallel outputs. Set All done only if running after failures is actually intended; otherwise the default requires success.
explanations.c:
Chaining tasks sequentially discards the requested parallel execution pattern.

Additional context:
Sequential edges serialize otherwise independent tasks. They can increase runtime and are not the stated parallel dependency pattern.
explanations.d:
Depending only on the SQL task leaves the dashboard free to run before the notebook and pipeline outputs are ready.

Additional context:
A missing edge means the dashboard is not constrained by the other two tasks. It could start while those outputs are still incomplete.

text:
A data engineer is designing a cost-optimized, event-driven pipeline. They configure a Lakeflow Job
with a File Arrival trigger to watch an S3 bucket. The job runs a notebook that uses Auto Loader with
trigger (availableNow=True) to ingest data into a Bronze table.
What is the technical relationship between the File Arrival trigger and Auto Loader in this integration
pattern?

choices.text:
Auto Loader must be configured in File
Notification mode to work with a Lakeflow
Job File Arrival trigger.

The File Arrival trigger starts the job run, while
Auto Loader uses its internal checkpoint to
independently identify and process only the
new files that have arrived since the last
successful commit.

The File Arrival trigger automatically passes
the specific file path of the new arrival to
Auto Loader, allowing the engineer to skip the
source path configuration in the code.

Using a File Arrival trigger requires the
engineer to disable Auto Loader's
checkpointing to prevent the job from
processing the same file multiple times.

originalKeyText:
b) The File Arrival trigger
starts the job run, while
Auto Loader uses its
internal checkpoint to
independently identify
and process only the
new files that have
arrived since the last
successful commit.

explanations.a:
File-arrival triggering and Auto Loader discovery modes are separate mechanisms; the job trigger does not require selecting Auto Loader File Notification mode.

Additional context:
File-arrival detection belongs to job orchestration, while discovery mode belongs to the ingestion reader. They are separate supported configuration choices.
explanations.b:
The job trigger detects arrivals and starts the run; Auto Loader then uses its own persisted state to process unprocessed files with AvailableNow.

Additional context:
AvailableNow then gives the ingestion run a bounded backlog to process. The checkpoint still defines what the reader has already committed, independently of why the job started.
explanations.c:
The trigger starts a job run; it does not let ingestion code omit its source path by automatically wiring an arriving file path into Auto Loader.

Additional context:
The job starts the configured notebook/task rather than rewriting its input path. The reader still needs its source configuration and progress state.
explanations.d:
Disabling checkpointing removes the state Auto Loader uses for recovery and tracking processed files. A file-arrival trigger does not replace that checkpoint or require disabling it.

Additional context:
Checkpoint state is what makes repeated runs and failures recoverable. Turning it off would not be a supported way to prevent duplicate processing.

text:
A Lakeflow Jobs workflow fails at the last task because of an error in a notebook task. This workflow
is scheduled to run daily. The data engineer fixes the notebook and wants to rerun the pipeline. This
workflow is very compute-intensive and expensive to run.
Which action should the data engineer take in order to minimize downtime and compute cost?

choices.text: Restart the cluster
Re-run the entire workflow
Switch to another cluster
Repair run

originalKeyText: d) Repair run

explanations.a: Restarting compute does not repair the failed job run or select which tasks need retry. It can add provisioning delay without completing the workflow.
explanations.b: A full rerun repeats successful work and can recreate substantial time and cost. The scenario explicitly wants to avoid that unnecessary repetition.
explanations.c: Changing clusters does not by itself resume the task graph. The reported cause is fixed notebook code, not a demonstrated compute defect.
explanations.d: Repair run resumes the failed portion of a supported multi-task job after the code fix. Successful prior tasks need not all be reexecuted.

text:
A data analyst has a series of queries in a SQL program. The data analyst wants this program to run
every day. They only want the final query in the program to run on Sundays. They ask for help from
the data engineering team to complete this task.
Which of the following approaches could be used by the data engineering team to complete this
task?

choices.text:
They could submit a feature request with
Databricks to add this functionality.

They could wrap the queries using PySpark
and use Python’s control flow system to
determine when to run the final query.

They could only run the entire program on
Sundays.

They could automatically restrict access to
the source table in the final query so that it is
only accessible on Sundays.

They could redesign the data model to
separate the data used in the final query into
a new table.

originalKeyText:
b) They could wrap the
queries using PySpark
and use Python’s control
flow system to
determine when to run
the final query.

explanations.a: The platform already supports Python orchestration of SQL, so a feature request is unnecessary. Notebook language support is not restricted to one rigid SQL program.
explanations.b: Wrapping SQL execution in Python allows a weekday check to guard the final query. Earlier statements can still run on every daily execution.
explanations.c: Running the entire program only on Sundays would skip required daily queries. It changes the schedule of every statement instead of only the last one.
explanations.d: Changing access permissions is a security operation rather than ordinary program control flow. It would also affect other consumers of the table.
explanations.e: Separating tables changes the data model but does not by itself decide when a query runs. The requirement concerns execution logic, not storage layout.

A pipeline uses COPY INTO to ingest CSV files from cloud object storage into a Unity Catalog Delta
table. Some files are occasionally re-uploaded with corrections using the same filename. The

Reload all files from the source path on each
run

Load corrections as new files and apply

Recreate the target table before each run
Overwrite the target Delta table on each run

table

explanations.a: Reloading every file can duplicate records and wastes work unless a carefully designed full-rebuild strategy is used. It is not the incremental correction approach requested.

text:

reads from this table continues running during the conversion. After the conversion completes,
the streaming job stops processing new records.
How should the data engineer resolve this?

choices.text:
Grant the streaming job additional
permissions on the new managed storage
location

Restart the streaming job, so it picks up the
new managed table location

Run REFRESH TABLE on the converted table
to update the streaming checkpoint

Delete the streaming checkpoint directory
and let the job reprocess from the beginning

originalKeyText:
b) Restart the streaming
job, so it picks up the
new managed table
location

explanations.a: Additional storage permissions are not the documented generic remedy for the conversion-related stopped stream. Investigate a real authorization error separately rather than assume one here.
explanations.b: B follows the conversion reference: restart the stream using its existing settings so it picks up the converted table/redirect. This preserves its recovery state.
explanations.c: REFRESH TABLE refreshes relation/cache metadata but does not rewrite or restart the streaming query’s checkpoint execution. It is not the documented stream recovery step.

originalKeyText:
b) The new userAgent field
is added as a new
nullable column in the
Delta table, populated
for new data.

explanations.a: New nullable columns do not require backfilling all old data to a non-null default. Older records typically read as NULL for the newly added field.

Events: Ingesting 5,000 events per second from an Apache Kafka topic. » Customer Master Data:
Syncing only changed records every 4 hours from a Snowflake database. The solution must meet

seconds. » Prevent the reprocessing of customer master data that has not changed.

full refresh for Snowflake.

Use file notification mode because it scales
efficiently for both large numbers of existing
files and continuous new arrivals by using
cloud storage events rather than repeatedly
listing directories.

Use directory listing mode because it
provides better performance for the initial
processing of 50,000 existing files through
optimized incremental listing capabilities.

Use directory listing mode initially to process

and continuous new
arrivals by using cloud

than repeatedly listing

A data engineer is designing a bronze-to-silver pipeline on the Databricks Data Intelligence
Platform. The source system sends daily CSV files, and over time, new optional columns are
added. The data engineer wants a storage format and table feature that together ensure the
following: » The table prevents writes that do not conform to the defined schema. + The table can
evolve its schema to include new optional columns without having to manually recreate the table.
» Previous versions of the table can be queried later for debugging and auditing.

schema inference and rely on re-running the

Use an external table with Auto Loader

and recreate the table whenever new

originalKeyText:

its native capabilities.

text:
A developer has configured Databricks Connect and starts running PySpark code locally. They
notice that Data Frame operations are executed on the remote cluster, but actions like . show()
return results directly in their local console.
What does this behaviour illustrate about how Databricks Connect is used?

It requires manual synchronization of results
from the cluster

It runs all Spark compute locally and only
reads remote files

It proxies Spark commands from the local
client to the remote cluster

It mirrors the entire cluster environment on
the developer's machine

originalKeyText:
c) It proxies Spark
commands from the
local client to the
remote cluster

explanations.a:
The client API returns results to the local program; manually synchronizing output is not the normal interaction described.

Additional context:
show or collect returns materialized results through the client connection. Manual copying is not the normal DataFrame result path.
explanations.b:
The heavy Spark computation runs on Databricks compute, rather than entirely on the developer’s laptop.

Additional context:
Local Python business logic can run on the client, but distributed Spark transformations are sent to the target. The distinction is explicit in the Connect architecture.
explanations.c:
Submitting Spark operations from the local client to remote compute explains why transformations execute remotely and results return to the local console.

Additional context:
The API constructs plans locally and submits them for remote execution. Actions then return their results to the local program as appropriate.
explanations.d:
Connect is a remote client interface; it does not replicate the entire cluster environment onto the local machine.

Additional context:
The client is intentionally thin and relies on remote runtime services. Recreating the entire cluster on the laptop would be a different architecture.

text:
A data engineer working in Databricks needs to control BI query latency and cost for a sales
analytics domain. Silver tables already contain validated, normalized sales and product data. The
team wants dashboard-friendly query performance and to align datasets with business concepts
(e.g., weekly sales and account_performance) without overloading analysts with complex joins.
Which design approach should a data engineer choose for the Gold layer in a medallion
architecture?

choices.text:
Move raw, append-on1y source data directly
into Gold to avoid transformation costs and
enable time travel.

Create denormalized, domain-aligned tables
and materialized aggregates (€.g.,
weekly_sales) optimized for reporting and
dashboards.

Build only lightly cleansed views in Gold and
preserve most business logic in Silver to
reduce duplication.

Keep all data heavily normalized in Gold to
minimize storage and rely on BI tools to join
data at query time.

originalKeyText:
b) Create denormalized,
domain-aligned tables
and materialized
aggregates (€.g.,
weekly_sales)
optimized for reporting
and dashboards.

explanations.a:
Raw append-only source fidelity is the Bronze role, not the dashboard-optimized Gold design requested.

Additional context:
Preserving raw fidelity belongs in Bronze rather than a dashboard-serving Gold model. Raw landing does not eliminate the need for a business representation.
explanations.b:
Denormalized domain-aligned tables and materialized aggregates directly match the documented Gold modeling and query-performance goals.

Additional context:
The source asks for named business metrics and avoiding repeated analyst joins. Precomputed domain-oriented outputs directly address those query and usability requirements.
explanations.c:
Light cleansing without a business-serving model does not meet the stated need to avoid complex analyst joins.

Additional context:
Light cleansing does not by itself supply the shared business measures described. Keeping all logic elsewhere can push unnecessary work into every dashboard query.
explanations.d:
Keeping everything heavily normalized and forcing BI to repeatedly join does not meet this scenario’s dashboard latency and simplicity requirements.

Additional context:
Normalization can be valuable in detailed models but is not the stated dashboard simplification goal. Relying on each BI query to reconstruct the business model misses that requirement.

text:
A data engineer wants to create an external table in Databricks that references data stored in an
Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) location. The goal is to enable Databricks to access and query
this external data without moving it into the Databricks-managed storage.
Which step should the data engineer take to successfully create the external table?

choices.text:
Use the CREATE MANAGED TABLE statement
and specify the LOCATION clause with the
path to the external data.

CREATE UNMANAGED TABLE statement
without specifying a LOCATION clause.

Use the CREATE TABLE statement and
specify the LOCATION clause with the path
to the external data.

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement without
specifying a LOCATION clause.

originalKeyText:
c) Use the CREATE TABLE
statement and specify
the LOCATION clause
with the path to the
external data.

explanations.a:
CREATE MANAGED TABLE is not the documented syntax for this external-location table, and managed storage is contrary to the scenario.

Additional context:
The requested source path is external data already present in ADLS. A managed-table declaration is not the source’s documented CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION approach.
explanations.b:
CREATE UNMANAGED TABLE without a location is not the documented external table syntax and does not identify the ADLS data.

Additional context:
An unsupported keyword does not become a table type merely because it sounds like the opposite of managed. A valid table definition also needs the intended source location.
explanations.c:
CREATE TABLE with LOCATION declares the external storage path; required external-location permissions and credentials must also be in place.

Additional context:
The catalog definition references the external data path under the configured authorization model. It does not copy the data into a managed storage root just by being registered.
explanations.d:
An external table definition must identify the data location; omitting LOCATION does not point Databricks to the specified ADLS data.

Additional context:
An external table still needs its data location established. The missing path prevents the statement from identifying the ADLS dataset in the scenario.

references.title: CREATE TABLE [USING]
references.section: Parameters — LOCATION
references.support: CREATE TABLE with a LOCATION references external data at that location rather than moving it into managed table storage.

keyConcept: CREATE TABLE with a LOCATION references external data at that location rather than moving it into managed table storage.
examTip: An external table requires a declared data location and appropriate storage permissions.
analysis: CREATE TABLE with a LOCATION references external data at that location rather than moving it into managed table storage.

text:
A data engineer is debugging a Python notebook in Databricks that processes a dataset using
PySpark. The notebook fails with an error during a DataFrame transformation. The engineer wants
to inspect the state of variables, such as the input DataFrame and intermediate results, to identify
where the error occurs.
Which tool should the engineer use to debug the notebook and inspect the values of variables like
DataFrames?

choices.text:
Use the Databricks CLI to download and
analyze driver logs for detailed error
messages

Use the Python Notebook Interactive
Debugger to set breakpoints and inspect
variable values in real-time

Use the Ganglia UI to monitor cluster
resource usage and identify hardware issues

Use the Spark UI to analyze the execution
plan and identify stages where the job failed

originalKeyText:
b) Use the Python
Notebook Interactive
Debugger to set
breakpoints and inspect
variable values in real-
time

explanations.a:
Downloaded logs can explain recorded failures but do not provide live breakpoint-based inspection of Python variables.

Additional context:
Logs can report exceptions and messages but cannot interactively inspect every current Python variable. They are useful supporting evidence rather than the debugger replacement.
explanations.b:
The interactive debugger explicitly supports breakpoints, stepping, and viewing variable values, matching the requested inspection workflow.

Additional context:
The paused source line and variable explorer expose the intermediate state the scenario asks for. Continue stepping to locate the operation that diverges or fails.
explanations.c:
Cluster resource monitoring diagnoses utilization, rather than exposing the notebook’s current Python variable state.

Additional context:
Hardware resource monitoring can reveal CPU/memory pressure. It does not show the live Python argument values at a breakpoint.
explanations.d:
Spark UI stages and query plans help diagnose distributed execution, but are not the requested source-level variable inspection tool.

Additional context:
Spark UI is useful for stages, plans, shuffles, and task failures. The requested notebook variable inspection is a different diagnostic granularity.

references.title: Debug Databricks notebooks
references.section: Start debugging; Debugging actions
references.support: The Python notebook debugger lets you pause at breakpoints and inspect variables while stepping through code.

keyConcept: The Python notebook debugger lets you pause at breakpoints and inspect variables while stepping through code.
examTip: Execution plans explain Spark work; a Python debugger reveals program state at a line.
analysis: The Python notebook debugger lets you pause at breakpoints and inspect variables while stepping through code.

text: What is the maximum output supported by a job cluster to ensure a notebook does not fail?

choices.text: 25MBs
10MBs
30MBs
15MBs

originalKeyText: b) 10MBs
issues: Research correction: source key B differs from documentation-supported answer C.

explanations.a: 25 MB is not the documented job-cluster notebook output maximum. A smaller chosen limit may be safe but is not the maximum asked for.
explanations.b: 10 MB is a newer runtime’s default cell output limit, not the documented total job notebook output maximum. The source B key conflates these limits.
explanations.c: C gives the documented 30-MB maximum notebook output size for job clusters. Monitor the combined output rather than assume each cell can independently use that whole amount.
explanations.d: 15 MB is neither the stated total notebook maximum nor the default cell limit in the cited reference. It does not answer the maximum question.

references.title: Known limitations of Databricks notebooks
references.section: Notebook cell outputs; Job cluster output limit
references.support: The current notebook limitations reference states a 30-MB maximum notebook output for job clusters. A 10-MB default can refer to individual cell output in newer runtimes, which is a different scope.

analysis: The current notebook limitations reference states a 30-MB maximum notebook output for job clusters. A 10-MB default can refer to individual cell output in newer runtimes, which is a different scope.
keyConcept: The current notebook limitations reference states a 30-MB maximum notebook output for job clusters. A 10-MB default can refer to individual cell output in newer runtimes, which is a different scope.
examTip: Always distinguish a cell’s configured output limit from the whole notebook’s job output limit.

text:
A data engineer is working on a personal laptop and needs to perform complex transformations
on data stored in a Delta Lake on cloud storage. The engineer decides to use Databricks Connect
to interact with Databricks clusters and work in their local IDE.
How does Databricks Connect enable the engineer to develop, test, and debug code seamlessly
on their personal laptop while interacting with Databricks clusters?

choices.text:
By providing a local environment that mimics
the Databricks runtime, enabling the
engineer to develop, test, and debug code
using a specific IDE that is required by
Databricks

By providing a local environment that mimics
the Databricks runtime, enabling the
engineer to develop, test, and debug code
only through Databricks’ own web interface

By allowing direct execution of Spark jobs
from the local machine without needing a
network connection

By providing a local environment that mimics
the Databricks runtime, enabling the
engineer to develop, test, and debug code
using their preferred IDE

originalKeyText:
d) By providing a local
environment that
mimics the Databricks
runtime, enabling the
engineer to develop,
test, and debug code
using their preferred
IDE
issues: Imprecise wording: Databricks Connect is a remote Spark client; it does not mirror the entire Databricks Runtime locally.

explanations.a: Connect is not restricted to a single required IDE, and the full runtime is not copied locally. Both claims misdescribe the client/server model.
explanations.b: Local IDE development is a principal Connect use case, not something limited to the web interface. A mirrored runtime is also not the documented mechanism.
explanations.c: Remote execution requires network connectivity and authentication. Connect does not execute remote Spark transformations without a connection.
explanations.d: Preferred-IDE development is supported, but the local environment does not mimic/replicate the full remote runtime. A corrected answer should describe a thin client with remote Spark execution.

references.title: Databricks Connect
references.section: How does Databricks Connect work?
references.support: Connect is a thin local client that sends Spark logical plans to remote compute; it does not mirror the entire Databricks Runtime on the laptop. D has the intended preferred-IDE idea but shares the false local-runtime-mirroring premise with A and B.

analysis: Connect is a thin local client that sends Spark logical plans to remote compute; it does not mirror the entire Databricks Runtime on the laptop. D has the intended preferred-IDE idea but shares the false local-runtime-mirroring premise with A and B.
keyConcept: Connect is a thin local client that sends Spark logical plans to remote compute; it does not mirror the entire Databricks Runtime on the laptop. D has the intended preferred-IDE idea but shares the false local-runtime-mirroring premise with A and B.
examTip: General client code runs locally; Spark transformations and UDF execution run remotely.

text:
Which compute option should be chosen in a scenario where small scale ad-hoc Python scripts
need to be run at high frequency and should wind down quickly after these queries have finished
running?

choices.text: All-purpose Cluster
Job Cluster
Serverless Compute
SQL Warehouse

originalKeyText: c) Serverless Compute

explanations.a: All-purpose compute supports ad hoc Python but requires more cluster lifecycle management and can remain idle. It is not the lowest-management fast-elastic option here.
explanations.b: Job clusters suit automated run lifecycles but introduce per-run provisioning and job orchestration for ad hoc work. They are not the direct managed interactive choice.
explanations.c: C supplies managed resource provisioning for supported Python workloads with less cluster administration. It best matches the short, frequent, low-management requirement.
explanations.d: A SQL warehouse is optimized for SQL execution, not arbitrary ad hoc Python scripts. It is the wrong execution interface for the stated language.

references.title: Run your Lakeflow Jobs with serverless compute for workflows
references.section: Serverless compute; Interactive and jobs lifecycle
references.support: Supported serverless Python execution reduces provisioning and manual lifecycle work for frequent small ad hoc tasks. Measure actual startup/idle behavior rather than assuming resources disappear instantly after every statement.

references.title: Compute
references.section: Serverless compute; Interactive and jobs lifecycle
references.support: Supported serverless Python execution reduces provisioning and manual lifecycle work for frequent small ad hoc tasks. Measure actual startup/idle behavior rather than assuming resources disappear instantly after every statement.

analysis: Supported serverless Python execution reduces provisioning and manual lifecycle work for frequent small ad hoc tasks. Measure actual startup/idle behavior rather than assuming resources disappear instantly after every statement.
keyConcept: Supported serverless Python execution reduces provisioning and manual lifecycle work for frequent small ad hoc tasks. Measure actual startup/idle behavior rather than assuming resources disappear instantly after every statement.
examTip: Choose general Python-capable compute, not a SQL-only serving endpoint.

text:
A data engineer is attempting to write Python and SQL in the same command cell and is running
into an error. The engineer believed it was possible to use a Python variable in a SQL select
statement.
Why does the command fail?

choices.text:
Databricks supports language
interoperability in the same cell but only
between Scala and SQL.

Databricks supports multiple languages but
only one per notebook.
Databricks supports one language per cell.

Databricks supports language
interoperability but only if a special
character is used.

originalKeyText:
c) Databricks supports
one language per cell.

explanations.a:
The documentation does not grant special same-cell interoperability only to Scala and SQL; language execution contexts remain separate.

Additional context:
Supported language cells are dispatched to their own execution contexts. There is no general special exception making mixed Scala/SQL source one interpreter.
explanations.b:
A notebook can contain multiple languages in separate cells, so the restriction is not one language for the entire notebook.

Additional context:
Notebook-level multilingual support is broader than cell-level execution. Separate cells can use different supported languages.
explanations.c:
A cell has a single language context; mixing bare Python and SQL in the same cell does not create a shared interpreter.

Additional context:
A %sql cell executes as SQL rather than making arbitrary Python statements part of SQL syntax. Explicit interfaces such as spark.sql handle SQL strings from Python instead.
explanations.d:
A language magic chooses that cell’s language; it does not generally make mixed Python/SQL statements and variables interoperable in the same cell.

Additional context:
A magic selects a language context; it is not an unrestricted variable-sharing bridge. Data can be exchanged through supported external/table/result mechanisms.

references.title: Develop code in Databricks notebooks
references.section: Code languages in notebooks — Mix languages
references.support: A cell executes in one language REPL; a language magic selects the interpreter rather than mixing Python and SQL statements in one cell.

keyConcept: A cell executes in one language REPL; a language magic selects the interpreter rather than mixing Python and SQL statements in one cell.
examTip: Different languages can share external data resources, but not arbitrary variables across REPLs.
analysis: A cell executes in one language REPL; a language magic selects the interpreter rather than mixing Python and SQL statements in one cell.

text:
An organization needs an optimized storage layer that supports ACID transactions and schema
enforcement.
Which technology should the organization use?

choices.text: Delta Lake
Unity Catalog
Cloud File Storage
Data lake

originalKeyText: a) Delta Lake

explanations.a:
Delta Lake extends Parquet files with a transaction log and provides ACID transactions and schema enforcement.

Additional context:
The transaction log tracks committed table state and enables versioned operations. This is the storage layer named by the required reliability guarantees.
explanations.b:
Unity Catalog is the governance layer, not the transaction/storage format that supplies the requested capabilities.

Additional context:
Governance controls who can access objects and tracks catalog metadata/lineage. It complements rather than replaces the table transaction protocol.
explanations.c:
Cloud object storage alone does not add Delta’s table-level ACID protocol or schema enforcement.

Additional context:
Raw files in object storage do not by themselves define an atomic multi-file table transaction or schema contract. A table layer must supply those semantics.
explanations.d:
A data lake describes a broader storage architecture; Delta Lake is the specific transactional storage technology named in the question.

Additional context:
A lake can contain many types of files and tables. The specific optimized transactional format in the options is Delta Lake.

references.title: What is Delta Lake in Databricks?
references.section: What is Delta Lake in Databricks?
references.support: Delta Lake is the optimized storage layer providing ACID transactions and schema enforcement.

keyConcept: Delta Lake is the optimized storage layer providing ACID transactions and schema enforcement.
examTip: Separate transactional storage (Delta Lake) from governance (Unity Catalog).
analysis: Delta Lake is the optimized storage layer providing ACID transactions and schema enforcement.

text: How can Git operations be performed outside of Databricks Repos?

choices.text: Commit
Pull
Merge
Clone

originalKeyText: d) Clone
issues: Ambiguous question: commit, pull, merge, and clone can all be performed with external Git tools. The source Clone key is not uniquely supported.

explanations.a: Commit records local changes in a Git repository and is available in external Git clients. It is not exclusive to Databricks.
explanations.b: Pull obtains remote changes in an external working copy as well as in Git folders. It can be performed outside the platform.
explanations.c: Merge combines branches through external Git tooling too. Current Databricks also supports merging in its own Git workflow.
explanations.d: Clone creates a working copy and is certainly possible externally, but it is not the only listed external operation. Therefore the source D key cannot be uniquely graded.

references.title: Create and manage Git folders
references.section: Git operations; External Git clients
references.support: Commit, pull, merge, and clone can all be performed using Git tools outside Databricks Git folders. The question’s single Clone key is not uniquely supported by its wording.

analysis: Commit, pull, merge, and clone can all be performed using Git tools outside Databricks Git folders. The question’s single Clone key is not uniquely supported by its wording.
keyConcept: Commit, pull, merge, and clone can all be performed using Git tools outside Databricks Git folders. The question’s single Clone key is not uniquely supported by its wording.
examTip: Outside Databricks describes where a Git client runs, not a limitation that leaves only clone possible.

text: Which two components function in the DB platform architecture’s control plane? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Virtual Machines
Compute Orchestration
Serverless Compute
Compute
Unity Catalog

originalKeyText:
b) Compute
Orchestration
,
e)
Unity
Catalog

explanations.a: Virtual machines executing workload code are compute resources. Their hosting account and lifecycle do not make the actual processing a control-plane function.
explanations.b: Compute orchestration schedules and manages resources from backend control services. It is a control-plane responsibility, distinct from executing the data tasks.
explanations.c: Serverless workloads execute in the serverless compute plane described by the architecture reference. Managed ownership does not convert their execution into the control plane.
explanations.d: Compute refers to processing the workload and belongs in the compute plane. It is not the administrative orchestration service.
explanations.e: Unity Catalog’s central governance/metastore service manages object metadata and permissions. Data storage and query enforcement/execution remain separate; this option does not mean every governed file resides in the control plane.

references.title: High-level architecture
references.section: Workspace architecture; Control plane and compute plane
references.support: Compute orchestration and the central Unity Catalog governance/metastore service are control-plane functions. Actual query/data processing, including serverless processing, runs in a compute plane rather than becoming control-plane work merely because Databricks manages it.

analysis: Compute orchestration and the central Unity Catalog governance/metastore service are control-plane functions. Actual query/data processing, including serverless processing, runs in a compute plane rather than becoming control-plane work merely because Databricks manages it.
keyConcept: Compute orchestration and the central Unity Catalog governance/metastore service are control-plane functions. Actual query/data processing, including serverless processing, runs in a compute plane rather than becoming control-plane work merely because Databricks manages it.
examTip: Databricks-managed does not mean control plane: serverless execution still has its own compute plane.

text: Which file format is used for storing Delta Lake Table?

choices.text: CSV
Parquet
JSON
Delta

originalKeyText: b) Parquet

explanations.a:
CSV is not the primary physical data-file format of a Delta table.

Additional context:
CSV can be an input format that is ingested into Delta. It does not become the primary Delta row-file encoding.
explanations.b:
The official overview states that Delta Lake extends Parquet data files with a file-based transaction log.

Additional context:
The transaction protocol and log add table state around those data files. Naming Parquet does not imply that a plain Parquet folder alone supplies Delta semantics.
explanations.c:
JSON can appear in transaction log metadata, but does not describe the primary table data-file format.

Additional context:
JSON log files record actions/metadata rather than the primary table rows. The question asks about data storage, not every file in the table directory.
explanations.d:
Delta is the transaction-aware table protocol, rather than the physical encoding of its main data files.

Additional context:
Delta names the transactional table format. Parquet is the more precise physical data-file answer among the choices.

references.title: What is Delta Lake in Databricks?
references.section: What is Delta Lake in Databricks?
references.support: Delta table data is primarily stored in Parquet files, with transaction metadata alongside it.

keyConcept: Delta table data is primarily stored in Parquet files, with transaction metadata alongside it.
examTip: The table format is Delta; the underlying data-file format is Parquet.
analysis: Delta table data is primarily stored in Parquet files, with transaction metadata alongside it.

text:
A data engineer is running code in a Databricks Repo that is cloned from a central Git repository. A
colleague of the data engineer informs them that changes have been made and synced to the
central Git repository. The data engineer now needs to sync their Databricks Repo to get the
changes from the central Git repository.
Which Git operation does the data engineer need to run to accomplish this task?

choices.text: Clone
Pull
Merge
Push

originalKeyText: b) Pull

explanations.a:
Clone creates a new copy; this engineer already has a working checkout that needs updating.

Additional context:
A new clone is appropriate for creating another working copy, not for updating this existing one. The engineer already has the central repository configured.
explanations.b:
Pull is the documented action to update notebooks and files from the remote repository.

Additional context:
Pull transfers the latest remote changes into the current working copy. Local conflicts may need resolution before the combined branch can be used.
explanations.c:
Merge combines branches but does not alone retrieve the colleague’s remote commits into this checkout.

Additional context:
Merging is useful for combining branch histories, but it is not alone the remote fetch/update operation requested. Pull addresses the stated remote-to-local direction.
explanations.d:
Push publishes local changes to the central remote, opposite to the required update direction.

Additional context:
Push is the local-to-remote publication operation. It does not retrieve the colleague’s already published changes.

references.title: Create and manage Git folders
references.section: Pull changes
references.support: Pull retrieves and applies central repository changes to an existing Databricks Git folder.

keyConcept: Pull retrieves and applies central repository changes to an existing Databricks Git folder.
examTip: Use Pull for central-to-local updates; Push moves changes in the other direction.
analysis: Pull retrieves and applies central repository changes to an existing Databricks Git folder.
